Software Engineering Practices

84 English operational guides in 12 families: when to use a practice, how to apply it, illustrative examples, verification, outputs and limitations. Historical source occurrences remain traceable.

W · PolimiO · OsmaniP · Pragmatic EngineerF · Fowler websiteB · Earlier booksN · NDSE2 chaptersPAT · Practices

Each practice is an editorial engineering guide. Select a technique that addresses an observed need, adapt it to the available authority and environment, and use its verification criteria to judge the local result. Related techniques and repeated historical occurrences do not establish independent evidence of effectiveness.

Explore 12 practice families

Choose a family to focus the catalogue, then open a practice for its procedure, example and checks. All entries remain readable without JavaScript.

F011 practices

Scope, Exploration and Accountability

Decide whether an AI-assisted result is a disposable experiment or a candidate for maintained software. Make the intended outcome, permitted effects and accountable owner explicit before promoting a promising prototype into a longer-lived system.

Explore this family →
F021 practices

Measurement and Operational Learning

Connect attempts, human work, waiting, rework and accepted outcomes in a common event record. Compare equivalent work and observation periods, include abandoned attempts, and use the result to identify a specific delivery constraint rather than treating generation activity as delivered value.

Explore this family →
F0314 practices

Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Keep an authorized work item bounded while choosing how planning, execution, retries and stopping operate. Separate a replaceable plan from its governing intention, preserve permission and budget limits across restarts, and escalate unresolved meaning instead of authorizing it through another attempt.

Explore this family →
F0411 practices

Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Turn a request into versioned obligations, scenarios and decisions that a maintainer can inspect. Expose consequential ambiguity, challenge contradictions, and keep implementation plans and diagnostic scores subordinate to the current authorized contract. Reopen affected decisions when the intention changes.

Explore this family →
F056 practices

Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Evaluate implementation alternatives, migrations and runtime observations against a shared intention. Preserve behavior and ownership while changing structure, record why alternatives were rejected, and check whether another maintainer can make the next meaningful change without avoidable complexity.

Explore this family →
F0610 practices

Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Define who may perform which operation on which data and target, then enforce the boundary outside the model. Combine dependency provenance, content inspection and controlled tool access while treating a scanner result, a permission decision and application correctness as different claims.

Explore this family →
F076 practices

Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Derive expected behavior from an authorized source that the candidate cannot rewrite. Use reproducible checks, independent negative cases and identifiable evidence bundles to inspect a result, while preserving the distinction between a passing check, complete assurance and an authorized acceptance decision.

Explore this family →
F086 practices

Critique, Review and Trust

Make a review objection identify a concrete assumption, defect, source or test. Match scrutiny to the impact of the change and the available review capacity, preserve unresolved reasons, and treat model agreement as a review observation rather than proof that the candidate is correct.

Explore this family →
F0913 practices

Context, Memory and Handoffs

Keep instructions, retrieved information, task state and authoritative decisions distinguishable. Attach locators, version scope, ownership and renewal triggers to reusable context so that another engineer can resume the work, challenge its assumptions and retain historical facts without applying superseded rules.

Explore this family →
F104 practices

Competence, Learning and Mentoring

Create opportunities for a learner to predict behavior, diagnose failures, explain invariants and review alternatives in their own words. Retain expert guidance and AI assistance while evaluating understanding and later transfer separately from the immediate success of an assisted task.

Explore this family →
F119 practices

Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Assign owners to work items and shared targets, bound work in progress, and route escalation to the person with the relevant authority. Introduce organizational support and automation according to observed constraints, including integration effort and review capacity, rather than the number of agents or courses delivered.

Explore this family →
F123 practices

Economics, Infrastructure and Work

Compare the complete cost and obligations of obtaining an accepted outcome, including setup, human review, rework, waiting and infrastructure. Record the assumptions and observation window behind an adoption choice, and revisit it when real evidence changes rather than treating automation as a required destination.

Explore this family →

PAT:001PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Plan-Then-Execute

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Separate an authorized objective from the agent's replaceable execution plan. Before changing code, identify the result, constraints, evidence and stopping conditions; then execute a bounded step and revise the plan from observations. Replanning can change the route, while changes to the intended behavior require an explicit, authorized delta.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make progress inspectable without letting implementation discoveries silently redefine what the requester approved.

When to use it

  • A change spans several dependent actions that need a visible order.
  • An agent must resume work without reconstructing its objective from scattered conversation.

When to avoid it

  • A single reversible action is already unambiguous and a separate planning document would add no useful decision.
  • The intended behavior is disputed; resolve that question before planning its implementation.

Before you start

  • A versioned task envelope naming scope, owner, permissions and accepted obligations.
  • A usable check for the next increment and an explicit time, action or cost budget.

How to apply it

  1. Record the intended outcome, exclusions and acceptance owner separately from implementation choices and working hypotheses.
  2. Break the route into meaningful increments, identifying dependencies, uncertain assumptions and the observation needed after each increment.
  3. Execute the next permitted increment; attach the changed candidate and observed result to the task record.
  4. Revise remaining steps when observations warrant it, preserving the prior plan and the reason for changing direction.
  5. Stop and request a decision when success would require a new obligation, broader effects, an unavailable permission or exhausted budget.

Illustrative example

An agent plans to add a read-only export endpoint, then discovers that the existing data service has no stable paging order. It may replace its query strategy and run ordering checks. It records that a proposed change to retention policy would alter the authorized objective and leaves that separate decision to the owner before proceeding.

What to check

  • Each completed step points to observable evidence rather than the agent's assertion that it is done.
  • The current candidate still satisfies the same approved objective after any replanning.
  • The stop record distinguishes an unresolved decision from a technical failure or acceptance.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned objective and replaceable plan with a short change history.
  • Increment evidence and any decision needed from the owner.

Risks and failure modes

  • A detailed plan can create false confidence when its assumptions were never checked.
  • Repeated replanning can hide lack of progress unless attempts and remaining budget stay visible.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:002PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Swarm Migration (Map-Reduce for Agents)

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Partition a migration into independently owned units, let workers propose bounded transformations, and integrate them against shared behavior checks. This optional companion variant is useful only when dependencies are understood and review capacity exists. Its value must be assessed from accepted migration outcomes, including coordination and integration work, rather than assumed parallel speedups.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Explore whether a repetitive migration can be distributed without losing behavioral consistency, ownership or a recoverable integration path.

When to use it

  • Many components need the same bounded transformation and can be checked separately.
  • A pilot can establish whether partitioning and review save meaningful end-to-end effort.

When to avoid it

  • The change depends on one unresolved architecture or policy decision shared by all components.
  • One maintainer cannot inspect or integrate the proposed work within the available time.

Before you start

  • An explicit partition map, common migration contract and compatibility checks.
  • Isolated write areas with one owner per target and a named integration owner.

How to apply it

  1. Run a representative unit first to expose hidden coupling, oracle gaps and the actual review burden.
  2. Define worker inputs, permitted targets, expected artifacts and stop conditions; reserve shared interfaces for a designated owner.
  3. Dispatch only independent units up to the capacity of checking and integration, recording assignments and leases.
  4. Collect each candidate with baseline identity, changed paths, compatibility evidence and unresolved exceptions.
  5. Integrate incrementally, rerun cross-unit behavior checks and suspend further dispatch if the pilot assumptions fail.

Illustrative example

A team considers migrating several isolated configuration readers to a common representation. Two readers form a pilot with stored behavior cases. One exposes a shared parser assumption, so its dependent readers remain serial. Independent readers can proceed in separate workspaces, while an integrator compares their accepted outputs and records the extra review time before expanding the batch.

What to check

  • No two active assignments can change the same logical target or silently diverge on the migration contract.
  • Per-unit checks and integration checks preserve the required old and new behavior.
  • The comparison includes rejected patches, coordination, review, elapsed time and follow-up work.

Expected outputs

  • Partition and dependency map with per-unit evidence bundles.
  • Integrated candidate, exceptions and an observed pilot cost record.

Risks and failure modes

  • Duplicating an incorrect transformation multiplies rework across the batch.
  • A large arrival rate can overload reviewers and increase the time to an accepted migration.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Quality, Architecture and Maintainability — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:003PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Background Agent CI

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Run a bounded agent task in a background continuous-integration context and publish a candidate with traceable checks. The task may prepare or repair work within its assigned scope, but a successful job is only evidence from that environment. Background execution, merge authority, production access and release approval remain separate decisions.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Use unattended execution where its trigger, permissions, artifacts and termination can be made explicit and reviewed later.

When to use it

  • A repeatable maintenance task can produce a reviewable patch without interactive clarification.
  • Existing CI can capture candidate identity, execution logs and scoped verification results.

When to avoid it

  • The task requires a product decision or access that cannot safely be delegated to that job.
  • The workflow would merge or release solely because the agent reports success.

Before you start

  • A trusted trigger, fixed input revision and restricted execution identity.
  • A task contract with budgets, allowed writes and an artifact retention policy.

How to apply it

  1. Specify the trigger and deduplicate repeated events so the same request does not start competing work.
  2. Create an isolated candidate workspace and supply only the credentials and operations needed for the permitted task.
  3. Execute the bounded change while retaining tool failures, attempts, checks and the final candidate identity.
  4. Publish a patch and evidence as review artifacts, with unresolved issues clearly separated from completed obligations.
  5. Route the result to the named reviewer; let a distinct authorized workflow decide merge, deployment or cancellation.

Illustrative example

A nightly job is allowed to refresh generated API examples from the current schema. It creates a branch, runs the example validator and uploads the diff. If the schema requires a change to the public contract, it stops with that question. Passing validation permits the reviewer to inspect the candidate; it does not cause the service to deploy.

What to check

  • The displayed checks belong to the exact candidate revision being offered for review.
  • A duplicate trigger, timeout or restart does not produce uncontrolled concurrent writes.
  • The job cannot acquire release permission from the contents of a repository file or model response.

Expected outputs

  • Reviewable candidate and checks tied to the triggering event.
  • Completion, hold or failure record with remaining obligations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Logs and artifacts can retain sensitive input beyond the intended task boundary.
  • An apparently healthy background job can create an unnoticed backlog of unreviewed candidates.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:004PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Initializer-Maintainer Dual Agent Architecture

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Distinguish initial setup from continued maintenance when the two activities require different context or permissions. An initializer establishes a reviewable starting state; a maintainer works from that accepted state under a narrower task contract. These are functional configurations that may share one agent implementation, not a requirement to deploy two autonomous agents.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent one-time scaffolding decisions and privileges from becoming an invisible permanent operating mode.

When to use it

  • Bootstrapping and routine changes have materially different write domains or information needs.
  • A long-running project needs a deliberate handoff from initial construction to maintenance.

When to avoid it

  • A single restricted workflow already handles setup and later work clearly.
  • The proposed split merely duplicates agents without changing permissions, evidence or ownership.

Before you start

  • An owner-approved definition of the initialized state and its verification.
  • Separate permission profiles and a handoff artifact tied to a concrete revision.

How to apply it

  1. Identify what belongs to setup: initial files, assumptions, dependencies, configuration and checks, with explicit limits on external effects.
  2. Run initialization with only the additional access it actually needs and record every resulting artifact and unresolved assumption.
  3. Check the initialized state independently of the initializer's completion list, then have the responsible owner accept or hold it.
  4. Remove temporary capabilities and provide the maintainer with current state, authoritative constraints and open questions.
  5. Treat any later need to repeat initialization as a new scoped request, preserving maintenance history and rechecking affected obligations.

Illustrative example

A starter workflow may create a repository skeleton and propose a dependency file. After review, a maintenance workflow receives permission to edit a feature directory and run local checks. It receives no package-publishing access. If a later task requires changing the build system, that becomes a separately reviewed scope change instead of quietly restoring the initializer's privileges.

What to check

  • The maintainer's effective permissions match its declared configuration after handoff.
  • The accepted initial revision and remaining uncertainties are recoverable without replaying chat history.
  • Setup checks cannot be substituted for evidence about a later maintenance candidate.

Expected outputs

  • Accepted setup manifest and explicit maintenance profile.
  • Handoff record containing current state, ownership and unresolved assumptions.

Risks and failure modes

  • A ceremonial two-agent design can increase coordination without reducing uncertainty.
  • Unreviewed setup defaults can become entrenched dependencies that later work treats as authoritative.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:001 · Plan-Then-Execute
  • PAT:072 · Handoff Chain
  • PAT:073 · Multi-Mode Agent

Suggested companion techniques for comparison or combination; these links do not assert validated effectiveness.

PAT:005PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Feature List as Immutable Contract

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Represent approved feature obligations as a versioned contract that the implementation process can consult but cannot silently rewrite. The contract is stable within a review revision, while approved changes create a new revision and impact assessment. A maker-maintained status field records progress; it is not independent acceptance evidence for the feature.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep generated code, tests and progress reporting anchored to the same approved behavioral obligations.

When to use it

  • Several implementation attempts must be compared against one stable feature definition.
  • A team needs to distinguish proposed requirements, accepted obligations and delivered evidence.

When to avoid it

  • The feature's decisive behavior is still unresolved and a frozen checklist would conceal the question.
  • The list is used as a substitute for scenarios, constraints or review judgment.

Before you start

  • Stable obligation identifiers with an owner, revision and approval record.
  • Scenarios or other independent expectations that explain what fulfilling each obligation means.

How to apply it

  1. State obligations in observable terms and separate them from suggested implementation steps, optional ideas and unresolved questions.
  2. Protect the approved revision from routine implementation writes; retain a readable source of authority and change process.
  3. Link candidate changes and checks to obligation identifiers, allowing incomplete or blocked states without rewriting the obligation.
  4. When scope legitimately changes, obtain the authorized delta and identify affected scenarios, code, evidence and earlier decisions.
  5. Present the completed candidate with its contract revision and evidence; let the designated acceptance authority make the final disposition.

Illustrative example

A feature list requires an export to omit archived records and preserve a stable ordering. The maker marks both items as implemented and links its checks. A reviewer discovers that archived records still appear under one filter. The contract stays unchanged, the first item returns to an unresolved state, and the candidate requires repair before acceptance.

What to check

  • Every completion claim identifies both the obligation revision and the evidence supporting it.
  • A status toggle cannot alter the approved expected behavior or overwrite a failed check.
  • Authorized deltas have an owner and an impact set, including previously accepted evidence that needs renewal.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned feature contract and approved change history.
  • Trace from each obligation to candidate evidence and acceptance disposition.

Risks and failure modes

  • Checkbox completion can hide interactions and nonfunctional obligations absent from the list.
  • Freezing a mistaken requirement indefinitely can turn traceability into resistance to necessary correction.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:061 · Consistency Analysis Gate
  • PAT:076 · Gate-Enforced Progression

PAT:006PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Context Window Anxiety Management

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Manage finite conversation context through explicit task state, selective retrieval and checked compaction. Observe practical symptoms such as lost constraints, repeated investigation or stale assumptions rather than diagnosing an agent's feelings. A smaller context is useful only if the resumed process retains the current objective, evidence, remaining work and permission boundaries.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep a long task resumable without relying on every prior conversation turn remaining available to the model.

When to use it

  • Work spans long sessions or repeated agent restarts with significant intermediate decisions.
  • Repeated rediscovery or forgotten constraints suggest the current context strategy is failing.

When to avoid it

  • A short task has little state and a checkpoint system would exceed its useful complexity.
  • The proposed summary omits unresolved questions merely to make the record appear complete.

Before you start

  • A typed state record separating approved intent, observations, candidate work and assumptions.
  • Versioned source locators and an owner who can resolve uncertain authority or stale information.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the minimum resume state: current revision, objective, limits, observations, unresolved questions, spent budget and next decision.
  2. Write a checkpoint before compaction, retaining links to fuller evidence instead of copying every log into the summary.
  3. Compare the checkpoint against authoritative task records and explicitly label uncertain or historical material.
  4. Resume from the checkpoint and retrieve detailed evidence only when the next action requires it.
  5. Check for repeated work, missed constraints and stale claims; revise the checkpoint format when a concrete information loss is found.

Illustrative example

A migration pauses after two of five modules pass compatibility checks. Its checkpoint names the source revision, completed modules, one unresolved parser assumption and the remaining budget. On restart, the agent reopens the parser evidence before changing the third module. It does not infer permission to widen the migration from a shortened summary saying only that work is unfinished.

What to check

  • A resumed worker can identify the next permitted action and outstanding decision without reconstructing the whole conversation.
  • Sampled evidence and current constraints survive compaction with their provenance and status intact.
  • Restarted work preserves spent budget and does not silently redo or contradict accepted increments.

Expected outputs

  • Compact resume record with versioned evidence links.
  • Observed compaction defects and a corrected state format.

Risks and failure modes

  • A polished summary can launder a tentative assumption into an apparent instruction.
  • Overcompaction can remove the counterexample or failed attempt needed to avoid repeating a mistake.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:029 · Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know
  • PAT:072 · Handoff Chain

PAT:007PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Compounding Engineering

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Turn experience from completed work into candidate reusable guidance, retaining the event, evidence, applicability and review history behind each lesson. Future tasks retrieve and evaluate that guidance in their own context. This is an operational memory practice; adding notes to a repository does not train model weights or guarantee that engineering performance improves.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make useful engineering experience available for later decisions without treating every past workaround as a permanent rule.

When to use it

  • Teams repeatedly encounter a diagnosable failure that could be prevented by a reusable check or instruction.
  • A completed change reveals an assumption worth preserving for maintainers.

When to avoid it

  • The task produced no verified observation beyond a plausible model explanation.
  • A temporary exception would be recorded as a universal instruction without review.

Before you start

  • An event record containing the attempted change, observed outcome and relevant versions.
  • An owner and review process for admitting, revising, invalidating or retiring guidance.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the specific situation, failed expectation and evidence before summarizing a proposed lesson.
  2. Separate the observation from the inferred recommendation, naming the conditions under which that recommendation might apply.
  3. Test the candidate guidance on a relevant case or obtain informed review; retain uncertainty when no evaluation is available.
  4. Publish approved guidance with its owner, scope, source links and triggers for renewal or invalidation.
  5. When reused, record whether it helped the new task and correct or retire it if the assumptions no longer hold.

Illustrative example

A team finds that a data export's nondeterministic ordering caused an intermittent comparison failure. It records the evidence and adds a scoped recommendation to make ordering expectations explicit in export tests. The note identifies the affected component and version. When another service retrieves the lesson, its maintainer checks the actual ordering contract before adopting the recommendation.

What to check

  • A reader can trace each recommendation to an observation and distinguish evidence from editorial inference.
  • The guidance states where it applies and how a later policy or dependency change could invalidate it.
  • Any claimed improvement uses observed accepted outcomes and includes maintenance cost and unsuccessful reuse.

Expected outputs

  • Reviewed lesson records with applicability and provenance.
  • Reuse observations and a visible retirement or correction history.

Risks and failure modes

  • A memorable anecdote may be mistaken for evidence of a generally effective method.
  • An accumulating rule set can increase context conflicts and maintenance burden instead of reducing them.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:016 · Structured Drift Detection
  • PAT:028 · Skills and Context Engineering: Remove Intent Debt
  • PAT:059 · Measurement & Learning

Suggested companion techniques for comparison or combination; these links do not assert validated effectiveness.

PAT:008PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Agent-Powered Codebase Q&A and Onboarding

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Use an agent to answer repository questions through identifiable code, tests, design decisions and current policy records. Answers should expose their evidence, uncertainty and version scope, then support a concrete understanding task. Retrieving the right passage and helping a maintainer predict or change behavior are separate outcomes that need different checks.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Reduce the cost of finding relevant knowledge while retaining a maintainer's ability to challenge the explanation and act on it.

When to use it

  • A newcomer needs a guided route through unfamiliar behavior and its ownership.
  • A maintainer must answer a bounded question about an existing implementation before proposing a change.

When to avoid it

  • The agent has no access to the current revision or the source needed for the question.
  • An answer would decide intended policy from observed legacy behavior without the policy owner's input.

Before you start

  • A known repository revision and accessible authoritative design or intention records.
  • A question with observable scope, plus a maintainer able to resolve missing context.

How to apply it

  1. State the question precisely, separating current behavior, intended behavior, historical rationale and how to make a change.
  2. Retrieve the smallest relevant set of code paths, tests and decisions, recording locators and applicable revisions.
  3. Construct an explanation that follows the behavior across boundaries and labels any unverified inference or missing source.
  4. Ask the learner to predict an outcome, locate a counterexample or explain an invariant using the retrieved evidence.
  5. Check that task against the code and contract, correct the explanation and preserve useful source links for future onboarding.

Illustrative example

A newcomer asks why a replayed request returns an older policy decision. The agent identifies the storage lookup, identity rule and approved replay invariant. The newcomer then predicts what happens for the same key with a changed payload and traces the conflict path. Finding those files is a retrieval success; making the correct prediction tests a different aspect of understanding.

What to check

  • Every material factual assertion has a locator that matches the revision under discussion.
  • The answer distinguishes a code observation from a requirement and states meaningful gaps.
  • The learner completes a behavior prediction or small change without merely repeating the agent's explanation.

Expected outputs

  • Code-anchored answer or short tour with uncertainty and ownership notes.
  • Separate retrieval and comprehension observations, plus any corrected explanation.

Risks and failure modes

  • Fluent summaries can conceal a missing call path or normalize an inherited defect.
  • Immediate confidence or successful copying can be mistaken for durable independent understanding.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:029 · Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know
  • PAT:048 · The Explainability Test
  • PAT:053 · Legacy Code Navigation

PAT:009PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

CI-as-Backpressure

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Use continuous-integration failures as a signal to limit further admission or repair within an existing task. A failed check can identify a concrete diagnostic and stop a branch from advancing until the relevant obligation is addressed. It does not enlarge the agent's scope, convert unrelated failures into assigned work or authorize changing the expected result.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent a stream of unchecked candidates from overwhelming verification and review while keeping repair decisions tied to evidence.

When to use it

  • Agents produce candidates faster than the team can verify or review them.
  • A required check supplies a concrete failure that can guide a bounded correction.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed response is to keep retrying an unexplained failure until one run passes.
  • The job failure concerns a separate component outside the authorized task.

Before you start

  • Explicit required checks and branch-progression rules owned by the project.
  • An attempt record linking candidate revision, failure diagnostic, scope and remaining budget.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the failing command, environment, candidate identity and relevant diagnostic before modifying anything.
  2. Classify whether the failure is introduced, pre-existing, environmental, uncertain or based on superseded expectations.
  3. For an in-scope defect, return a narrowly described repair request with the unchanged contract and protected oracle.
  4. Hold admission or progression according to the established policy while the required evidence is missing.
  5. Escalate unrelated or unexplained failures to their owner, preserving the failed result and the reason further work stopped.

Illustrative example

A documentation-generation agent produces a candidate whose required example validator fails on one changed code sample. The agent may repair that sample and rerun its checks. A separate database integration job also fails because its service is unavailable. The record classifies the infrastructure failure and holds the required status; it does not rewrite database code to make the dashboard green.

What to check

  • A retry follows a named diagnostic and is charged to the same persistent budget.
  • The branch cannot advance using a passing result from a different revision or a removed required check.
  • The hold identifies the missing evidence and the role able to resolve it.

Expected outputs

  • Failure classification with a bounded repair or escalation record.
  • Current verification status and admission or progression decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • Optimizing for a green dashboard can encourage weakening checks or hiding failures.
  • An unchecked inflow of candidates can move the bottleneck into review despite fast local repairs.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:026 · Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality
  • PAT:036 · CI Sweeper: classify before fixing

PAT:010PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Inference-Healed Code Review

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Turn a review finding into a bounded repair only after identifying the affected behavior and checking the finding's basis. The maker proposes a correction, reruns relevant evidence and returns the changed candidate for review. The loop treats AI comments as testable hypotheses, retaining dismissed findings and unresolved uncertainty instead of assuming the reviewer is correct.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make review feedback actionable without letting comment generation become an unexamined source of new requirements.

When to use it

  • A reviewer identifies a reproducible defect, contradicted invariant or concrete gap in the candidate's evidence.
  • A bounded repair can be evaluated under the existing approved task.

When to avoid it

  • The comment is a stylistic preference with no applicable project rule or meaningful consequence.
  • The proposed fix changes intended behavior and requires a decision from a different authority.

Before you start

  • The exact reviewed candidate and a finding with a locator, rationale and confidence boundary.
  • Protected acceptance expectations and a named reviewer responsible for the returned candidate.

How to apply it

  1. Reproduce the finding or identify the evidence that could distinguish a real defect from a mistaken hypothesis.
  2. Classify the comment as confirmed, disputed, informational or requiring an authority decision; record the reason.
  3. For a confirmed in-scope defect, create a narrow repair that preserves the approved behavior and unrelated code.
  4. Run the focused counterexample and the relevant regression checks against the new candidate.
  5. Return the diff and fresh evidence, linking the original finding and any remaining dispute for an explicit review disposition.

Illustrative example

An AI reviewer warns that replay reads the current policy threshold. The maintainer traces the path and reproduces a failure with a stored older decision. The maker repairs that path and reruns the replay and new-request checks. A separate comment about a possible duplicate transaction is dismissed with the documented conflict behavior, preserving the rationale instead of silently accepting every suggestion.

What to check

  • A substantive fix has a diagnostic that fails on the defective candidate and is addressed by the repaired one.
  • The reviewed revision and supporting evidence are current after the repair.
  • Dismissed or unresolved findings retain reasons so apparent silence is not mistaken for verification.

Expected outputs

  • Finding-to-repair trace with reproduction evidence and a bounded diff.
  • Fresh review bundle and disposition of each material finding.

Risks and failure modes

  • Repeated self-consistent explanations can reinforce the same incorrect interpretation.
  • Repairing low-value comments indiscriminately can consume the attention needed for consequential defects.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:027 · Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance
  • PAT:052 · Review Gauntlet
  • PAT:074 · Anti-Sycophancy Enforcement

Suggested companion techniques for comparison or combination; these links do not assert validated effectiveness.

PAT:011PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Reward Shaping for Tool Use

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Distinguish training-time reward design from the feedback an operating agent receives after a tool action. This retained conceptual entry helps teams identify what intervention they are actually proposing and what evidence it would require. It is outside the book's execution procedure: ordinary test failures and retry instructions are operational feedback, not proof that model parameters are being trained.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid applying the language of reward optimization to a workflow change that only changes prompts, tools, checks or retries.

When to use it

  • A proposal claims that rewarding tool use will improve the agent and needs a precise intervention definition.
  • A reviewer must compare a training proposal with a simpler runtime correction.

When to avoid it

  • The immediate task is an ordinary bounded repair that an existing diagnostic can guide.
  • There is no controlled training capability, data governance or credible evaluation plan.

Before you start

  • A clear statement of whether parameters, runtime instructions or orchestration behavior would change.
  • A separately governed evaluation plan with relevant outcomes and a credible comparison condition.

How to apply it

  1. Classify the proposed mechanism before designing a solution: training update, reward-model evaluation or runtime feedback.
  2. Define the actual desired outcome, such as a correctly completed permitted task, separately from a proxy like tool-call count.
  3. Identify how the proxy could be satisfied while the engineering outcome fails, including unnecessary calls or suppressed errors.
  4. Require evidence that evaluates unseen relevant tasks, permitted effects and full workflow cost before adopting a training claim.
  5. Keep any training experiment under a separate owner and process; use the book's bounded execution controls for the operational workflow regardless.

Illustrative example

A team proposes to reward an agent whenever a test passes. Inspection shows that its current setup merely inserts the test result into the next prompt; no training process exists. The proposal is renamed an execution-feedback loop. If the team later considers training, it must independently test whether the signal encourages correct behavior rather than editing expectations or avoiding difficult cases.

What to check

  • The intervention description correctly identifies what changes and what remains fixed.
  • The evaluation distinguishes the desired outcome from the proxy and includes plausible ways to exploit that proxy.
  • Any claimed improvement has evidence beyond the examples used to construct the intervention.

Expected outputs

  • Intervention classification and decision to use runtime feedback or assess a separately governed training proposal.
  • Evaluation questions and explicit evidence gaps.

Risks and failure modes

  • Calling all positive feedback a reward can hide the absence of a training mechanism.
  • A convenient scoring signal can favor behavior that looks successful while missing scope, correctness or authority.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:012PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

AI-Accelerated Learning and Skill Development

Family. Competence, Learning and Mentoring

Use AI assistance within a deliberate learning task that preserves the learner's own prediction, explanation, diagnosis and repair. A mentor can adjust the assistance and inspect reasoning, while later unaided work tests transfer. Faster completion of the assisted task is recorded separately from learning; no general gain in skill or retention follows from the practice name.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make assistance serve a stated learning objective while keeping evidence of independent reasoning visible to the learner and mentor.

When to use it

  • A newcomer needs to understand an invariant or unfamiliar subsystem before owning changes.
  • A team wants to evaluate whether its assisted workflow preserves opportunities for skill development.

When to avoid it

  • The learner only copies a completed answer and no independent reasoning task is planned.
  • An urgent delivery task cannot accommodate teaching; record that limitation rather than claiming it as training.

Before you start

  • A specific competence target and a mentor able to evaluate the reasoning.
  • A suitable exercise and a distinct later task for checking unaided transfer.

How to apply it

  1. Ask the learner to predict behavior or propose a diagnostic before revealing an assisted answer.
  2. Provide limited help appropriate to the observed difficulty, such as a code locator, explanation or counterexample.
  3. Have the learner repair or extend the candidate and explain the governing invariant in their own terms.
  4. Review the reasoning and the software result separately, recording what help was used and what remains uncertain.
  5. Return later with a different unaided task that needs the same underlying concept, then adjust the mentoring approach from the observation.

Illustrative example

A learner predicts how an old request should replay after a policy change. The assistant locates the storage code, and a senior asks the learner to identify a deliberately wrong implementation. The learner constructs a failing example and repairs it. On a later task with a different state transition, the mentor checks whether the learner can apply the same reasoning without the earlier hints.

What to check

  • The learner's prediction, explanation or diagnostic exists separately from the assistant's generated text.
  • Correct code is checked against the contract independently of the educational assessment.
  • The record distinguishes immediate assisted success, unaided performance and any later follow-up that is still unknown.

Expected outputs

  • Learning objective, assistance record and mentor feedback.
  • Independent-task observations with explicit limits on retention claims.

Risks and failure modes

  • A fluent explanation may create confidence without a transferable mental model.
  • Comparing unmatched exercises or learners can falsely attribute improvement to the assistant.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Developer Learning, Mentoring and Comprehension Debt — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:050 · Learning Loop Preservation

PAT:013PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Agent Reinforcement Fine-Tuning

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Treat reinforcement fine-tuning for an agent as a separate model-development proposal, outside the book's operational execution scope. Before considering it, define the observed failure, identify whether context or orchestration can address it, and specify an independent evaluation. A new model variant still needs the same external permissions, budgets, protected expectations and accountable acceptance process.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep a specialized training decision from becoming an assumed prerequisite for solving ordinary engineering workflow problems.

When to use it

  • A model-development team proposes fine-tuning as a response to a recurring, well-characterized agent failure.
  • A reviewer needs to compare that proposal with simpler changes to context, tools or verification.

When to avoid it

  • The failure is caused by missing authority, stale data or an inadequate oracle.
  • There is no separately authorized model-development process or relevant independent evaluation data.

Before you start

  • A reproducible failure description and baseline model or workflow version.
  • Named ownership for training data, evaluation, cost, access and any deployment decision.

How to apply it

  1. Describe the failed engineering outcome and separate model behavior from failures of inputs, permissions or surrounding systems.
  2. Evaluate whether a scoped runtime intervention can answer the problem before proposing a change to model parameters.
  3. For a genuine training proposal, require an explicit objective, data provenance and a held-out evaluation appropriate to the task.
  4. Compare candidates under the same authorized tasks and controls, retaining failures, review effort, costs and uncertainty.
  5. Adopt, hold or reject the proposal through its own governance process; retain the external execution and acceptance boundaries for any deployed variant.

Illustrative example

An agent repeatedly chooses an outdated API and the team considers fine-tuning. Investigation finds that its retrieved documentation comes from an obsolete dependency revision. The team corrects retrieval and reevaluates the workflow first. A later training proposal, if still warranted, must demonstrate value on distinct relevant tasks and cannot use the proposed model's own judgments as the sole acceptance evidence.

What to check

  • The diagnosed failure remains after correcting obvious context or orchestration defects.
  • The comparison separates training examples from independent evaluation and states what has not been established.
  • The deployed model cannot override tool permissions or declare its own changes accepted.

Expected outputs

  • Training-proposal decision with alternative interventions and evidence gaps.
  • Evaluation and deployment requirements owned outside the ordinary task loop.

Risks and failure modes

  • A training investment can mask an unresolved contract or poor information supply.
  • Narrow evaluation gains can be overgeneralized to different repositories, task classes or operational consequences.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Model-limit context; this training variant remains outside core execution
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:011 · Reward Shaping for Tool Use
  • PAT:030 · Connectors and Tools: Move Exact Work Outside the Weights
  • PAT:065 · Model Switching for Regeneration

PAT:014PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Deterministic Failure Harness

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Build a repeatable failure harness around a concrete behavioral obligation, fixing the relevant candidate, inputs, expected results and environment. The harness makes a selected defect inspectable and supports bounded repair. Its repeatability is conditional on controlled dependencies and the oracle's quality; it is not evidence that all defects are captured or that the system is generally deterministic.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn an ambiguous failure report into a diagnostic that another reviewer can reproduce and use to assess a repair.

When to use it

  • A candidate violates a known invariant and the failure can be isolated without changing the required behavior.
  • A repair loop needs a stable diagnostic instead of vague reviewer disapproval.

When to avoid it

  • The intended outcome is unresolved and the harness would freeze an unapproved assumption.
  • The test arrangement removes the boundary or timing condition responsible for the actual defect.

Before you start

  • Expected behavior derived from an authorized source independently of the faulty candidate.
  • Versioned fixtures, commands and environment details sufficient to explain the run.

How to apply it

  1. Name the obligation and select a minimal counterexample that distinguishes required behavior from the observed defect.
  2. Control relevant state, clocks, randomness and dependency versions where the test permits it, recording remaining variability.
  3. Verify that the defective candidate fails for the intended reason, not because setup or infrastructure is broken.
  4. Apply a bounded repair and run the same protected expectations against the new candidate.
  5. Retain the old failure, new result and environment record, then add wider checks for affected behavior without claiming exhaustive coverage.

Illustrative example

A replay bug appears only after reopening a service under a new policy. The harness stores a first decision, closes the service, reopens it with the new policy and checks the original response identity. The faulty candidate fails that invariant. A repaired candidate must pass the same expectation, while a separate new-request case checks that current policy still applies where intended.

What to check

  • A known defective candidate is rejected by the intended assertion, providing a meaningful negative control.
  • Repeated runs under the documented conditions have explainable outcomes and expose unresolved sources of variation.
  • Passing the harness leaves untested behavior and any production-environment differences explicitly visible.

Expected outputs

  • Reproducible failure fixture and protected expectation with provenance.
  • Candidate-bound run records and a statement of remaining coverage limits.

Risks and failure modes

  • Over-mocking can remove the interaction that causes the defect in the real system.
  • Changing expected results during repair can produce a repeatable but circular demonstration of success.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:015PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Regression Safety Net

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Maintain a regression set that checks both the newly authorized behavior and existing obligations left unchanged by the task. Identify each expectation's applicable revision and record the baseline result before interpreting a failure. Pre-existing defects remain visible and require classification; discovering them does not automatically authorize repairs outside the current scope.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Show that a bounded change satisfies its new obligation without silently breaking behavior the owner expected to preserve.

When to use it

  • A maintenance change affects behavior with existing users, stored history or compatibility obligations.
  • An authorized policy delta changes some expected results while leaving other invariants intact.

When to avoid it

  • The suite simply mirrors the implementation and has no independently justified expectations.
  • Historical failures are being removed or rewritten solely to make the current candidate appear healthy.

Before you start

  • An identified baseline and a record of the current suite's results.
  • Versioned obligations and a candidate impact map that a maintainer can challenge.

How to apply it

  1. Run or inspect the baseline checks and preserve failures, skipped coverage and environment limitations.
  2. Classify expectations as unchanged invariants, revised behavior, historical behavior or uncertain requirements.
  3. Add targeted cases for the authorized delta and its boundaries while protecting expectations that should remain unchanged.
  4. Run the required regression suite on the candidate, investigating unexpected failures without assuming every failure was introduced by the patch.
  5. Present baseline and candidate outcomes with failure classifications, impact reasoning and unresolved decisions for acceptance review.

Illustrative example

A policy change lowers a limit for new requests. The regression set checks the new threshold, unchanged high-risk handling and replay of an older stored decision. One unrelated formatting test was already failing on the baseline. The maintainer records that separately and applies the project's progression policy; the agent cannot silently reformat an unrelated module simply because it encountered the failure.

What to check

  • Each changed expected result traces to an authorized delta rather than the candidate's observed output.
  • Both newly required behavior and unaffected invariants have relevant checks.
  • The report preserves pre-existing and unexplained failures, including whether they block the current decision.

Expected outputs

  • Version-scoped regression matrix and baseline comparison.
  • Candidate results, impact assessment and classified outstanding failures.

Risks and failure modes

  • A narrow impact map can omit a hidden consumer, so selected checks may need broader regression evidence.
  • Treating old behavior as inherently correct can preserve a bug as a permanent contractual expectation.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:016PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Structured Drift Detection

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Detect when a retained instruction, assumption, test expectation or knowledge record no longer applies to current work. Compare explicit versions and validity scopes, assign an owner to resolve the difference, and trace affected decisions. Superseded material remains available for historical explanation while being excluded from decisions that require the current rule.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent a resumed task from treating yesterday's valid information as today's governing instruction.

When to use it

  • Policy, dependencies or interfaces have changed since a memory card or instruction file was written.
  • Several artifacts describe the same obligation and may have diverged in meaning or effective revision.

When to avoid it

  • The system discards old facts even when historical behavior still depends on them.
  • A simple textual mismatch is treated as sufficient authority to rewrite code or approved expectations.

Before you start

  • Records with source, revision, owner, validity scope and known renewal triggers.
  • A current authoritative reference and a way to record disputed or unknown status.

How to apply it

  1. Compare the task's current contract and environment against the applicability recorded on instructions, evidence and memory.
  2. Mark suspected drift explicitly, distinguishing superseded current guidance from historically valid observations.
  3. Trace candidate impacts through consumers, tests, decisions and handoffs; ask the responsible owner to challenge missing relationships.
  4. Refresh only the affected guidance and evidence under the authorized revision, retaining the prior record and reason for invalidation.
  5. Before resumed execution, verify that the selected context no longer presents stale or disputed material as current authority.

Illustrative example

A memory card says that new requests use an earlier approval threshold. A policy delta changes that threshold, but older stored decisions must still replay unchanged. The steward marks the card superseded for new requests, retains it for historical explanation and identifies tests needing renewal. The agent cannot solve the drift by deleting every reference to the former rule.

What to check

  • Current, historical, disputed and unknown claims are distinguishable in the retrieved context.
  • Each semantic correction has an accountable owner and an applicable revision.
  • Affected checks are renewed against the current candidate, while historical evidence remains traceable.

Expected outputs

  • Drift and invalidation register with owners and candidate impacts.
  • Refreshed context or expectations plus preserved superseded records.

Risks and failure modes

  • A dependency graph can miss a consumer and give an incomplete appearance of impact coverage.
  • Automatically selecting the newest text can privilege an unauthorized edit over an older authoritative decision.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:007 · Compounding Engineering

PAT:017PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Blast Radius Containment

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Limit the consequences of an agent mistake by enforcing permitted reads, writes, external operations, resource use and duration outside the model's own requests. Design containment for the actual task and test representative denials. The result is a constrained execution profile whose residual weaknesses remain explicit, not a claim of absolute security or complete isolation.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep a plausible but incorrect action from reaching assets or effects that the task has no authority to change.

When to use it

  • A tool-using agent can write files, access sensitive resources or call external services.
  • Different work phases require different capabilities and should not share every possible privilege.

When to avoid it

  • A prompt is the only barrier protecting a consequential resource.
  • The proposed isolation claim is based solely on a local simulation rather than the effective deployment controls.

Before you start

  • A task-specific threat and effect map naming protected assets and accountable owners.
  • An execution layer able to enforce and revoke the selected permissions independently of generated text.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the exact targets, operations, data and duration needed for the task, including indirect effects through tools.
  2. Configure the narrowest adequate execution profile, separating read-only discovery, candidate writes and any separately authorized external action.
  3. Protect the contract, expected results and credentials from the maker's write domain.
  4. Exercise representative permitted and forbidden actions, retaining denial evidence and any enforcement gaps.
  5. Monitor actual effects and stop or revoke access when a request crosses scope, expires or exposes an unresolved boundary.

Illustrative example

An agent may inspect source files, write a candidate in a dedicated workspace and run checks against synthetic data. A request to rewrite protected expected results is denied by the execution layer, even if the agent says the change is needed to finish. The operator verifies the actual filesystem and credential controls separately from the demonstration that the broker rejects a sample request.

What to check

  • Effective permissions match the declared task profile, including inherited credentials and network access.
  • Negative tests cover meaningful forbidden reads, writes or operations and record the enforcement component.
  • Timeout, cancellation and revocation stop new effects without resetting or broadening the original authority.

Expected outputs

  • Execution profile with tested allowed and denied operations.
  • Effect and denial log with residual enforcement limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • A permitted tool can expose a broader operation than its harmless-looking name suggests.
  • Isolation of files alone can leave shared databases, services or cost-bearing operations outside the containment boundary.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:018PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

PII and Secret Scrubbing

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Reduce unnecessary exposure of personal information and secrets before material enters an agent's context, logs, artifacts or external destination. Combine data minimization, scoped detection, controlled replacement and handling rules. Scrubbing is an imperfect transformation: a clean scan does not authorize sharing, and retained logs or re-identification clues can still cross the original data boundary.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Give the task the least sensitive adequate input while preserving the permissions and retention rules that apply to the source data.

When to use it

  • A debugging or documentation task can use synthetic or minimized examples instead of raw production records.
  • Potentially sensitive text would otherwise be copied into prompts, diagnostics or shared artifacts.

When to avoid it

  • The destination or operation is not authorized even if selected values are removed.
  • The task requires identifying information but its access and retention conditions have not been established.

Before you start

  • A classification of the relevant data and the allowed destinations, purposes and retention periods.
  • A controlled transformation path that does not leak originals into temporary files or logs.

How to apply it

  1. Map where input may travel, including model context, tool arguments, failures, caches and exported evidence.
  2. Prefer synthetic or reduced data when it can answer the same engineering question.
  3. Apply appropriate detection and transformation rules, preserving relationships only when they are needed and permitted.
  4. Review the transformed result for missed sensitive content and for distortions that would invalidate the task's conclusions.
  5. Use the approved destination and handling process; retain or remove intermediates according to the source's actual rules.

Illustrative example

A maintainer needs an example request that reproduces a parser defect. They construct a synthetic record with the same problematic structure instead of uploading a customer log. A checker confirms that the defect still reproduces. The remaining diagnostic is reviewed for embedded credentials and retained only in the approved task record; passing the scanner does not authorize posting it to an unrelated service.

What to check

  • The minimized input still reproduces the behavior relevant to the task.
  • Checks cover the output and incidental artifacts, with known detector limitations recorded.
  • The data owner or applicable authorization permits the destination and use independently of the scrub result.

Expected outputs

  • Minimized or synthetic task input with a transformation record.
  • Handling decision and residual sensitivity or fidelity limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Rare values and combinations can reveal information even after obvious identifiers are removed.
  • A debugging trace or exception can reintroduce an original value after the input was successfully scrubbed.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:019PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Subagent Spawning and Fan-Out

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Delegate bounded, genuinely independent subtasks when their outputs can be integrated and checked within available capacity. Each subagent receives a clear target, contract revision, permissions, evidence requirements and stopping rule. Fan-out is a conditional coordination choice; the right concurrency follows dependencies and reviewer load, not a fixed or maximized worker count.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Use concurrency to address a real partitionable workload while preserving ownership and a coherent final result.

When to use it

  • Read-only investigations or implementation units have distinct questions and explicit integration points.
  • The coordinator can review and reconcile the expected outputs without creating a larger bottleneck.

When to avoid it

  • Several workers would need to resolve the same open policy decision.
  • The subtasks share an uncontrolled mutable target or exceed the available checking capacity.

Before you start

  • A dependency and ownership map with a named coordinator.
  • A shared authorized objective and bounded per-worker access, budget and expected output.

How to apply it

  1. Identify which work is independent and what must remain serial, including shared interfaces and authority decisions.
  2. Assign each worker a distinct deliverable, required source revision and criteria for returning evidence or escalating uncertainty.
  3. Limit concurrency according to execution and review capacity, reserving time to integrate and verify results.
  4. Track progress and reassignment explicitly; cancel or hold affected workers if the contract changes or a dependency is invalidated.
  5. Integrate the outputs against the common objective and rerun checks that cross worker boundaries before presenting the final candidate.

Illustrative example

One worker inventories a public API, another inspects its tests, and a third investigates a separate documentation gap. Their tasks are read-only and each returns source locators and uncertainties. The coordinator uses those findings to assign one implementation owner. It does not dispatch three competing edits to the same API merely because three agents are available.

What to check

  • Each active worker can name its unique target, input revision and exit condition.
  • The coordinator detects duplicate logical work and invalidates stale assignments after a relevant change.
  • The integrated result has cross-boundary evidence beyond the individual workers' completion claims.

Expected outputs

  • Assignment and dependency record with bounded worker outputs.
  • Integrated evidence and a decision on whether concurrency was worth its coordination cost.

Risks and failure modes

  • Workers can agree on an incorrect shared assumption and make that error appear corroborated.
  • Unbounded fan-out can spend budget and reviewer attention before useful intermediate findings are available.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:031 · Worktrees: Isolate the Write Domains
  • PAT:032 · Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target
  • PAT:056 · Parallel Work Orchestration

PAT:020PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

File-System as State Machine

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Represent long-running task state in explicit durable artifacts with validated transitions, controlled writes and recoverable history. The filesystem is a storage substrate, not the state machine's authority. Correct operation also requires ownership, schema validation, concurrency handling and a clear account of what was committed before interruption or restart.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a task's current state and legal next action reconstructable without trusting a conversational claim that a stage completed.

When to use it

  • A task must pause, resume or hand off while preserving attempts, evidence and remaining budget.
  • Several processing stages need explicit input, output and completion identities.

When to avoid it

  • Multiple writers overwrite the same status file without a concurrency or ownership protocol.
  • The mere presence of a file is interpreted as proof of approval or successful execution.

Before you start

  • A state schema with named transitions, required evidence and a responsible writer.
  • A write and recovery mechanism appropriate to the storage system and concurrency model.

How to apply it

  1. Define states such as active, waiting for evidence, held and ready for review, separating them from acceptance decisions.
  2. Associate each transition with the task, candidate revision, prior state, event identity and required supporting artifacts.
  3. Validate proposed updates and commit them through the controlled writer, retaining enough history to identify partial or repeated events.
  4. On restart, reconcile the durable state with actual artifacts and execution results; preserve spent budget rather than starting a new allowance.
  5. Reject stale, conflicting or unsupported transitions and route uncertain recovery to the designated owner.

Illustrative example

A task writes a candidate and begins a check, then the process stops before recording the result. On restart, the state reader finds no completed evidence event for that candidate. It does not mark the task ready merely because a log file exists. The controller verifies the artifacts, records the interrupted attempt and reruns the required check within the remaining budget.

What to check

  • Interrupted updates and duplicate events leave an explainable state rather than a false completion marker.
  • Only the intended writer can change protected state or authoritative records.
  • A resumed task can recover candidate identity, unresolved work, prior failures and cumulative budget.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned state and event records with artifact references.
  • Recovery procedure and explicit unsupported or disputed transitions.

Risks and failure modes

  • A compact status file can drift from the actual files unless transitions bind their identities.
  • A homemade journal can appear robust in sequential tests while failing under concurrent or interrupted writes.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:021PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Tool Call Budget

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Cap tool use as one dimension of a bounded agent task and enforce the counter outside the model. Record consumed calls across retries, subprocesses and restarts, and check the remaining allowance before dispatch. A call limit controls activity, but calls differ in cost, duration and external effects, so it is not a complete spending or authority limit.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent unnoticed repeated tool activity and make the decision to spend another attempt explicit and inspectable.

When to use it

  • An autonomous task can repeatedly retrieve, test or invoke tools without a person deciding each step.
  • Several workers or restarts must share one cumulative task allowance.

When to avoid it

  • A call counter is being used as the only control over external writes or high-cost operations.
  • The task cannot observe tool usage reliably enough to enforce its stated cap.

Before you start

  • A controller-visible accounting rule for attempted, failed and delegated calls.
  • Separate task limits for time, cost, resource use or effects where those dimensions matter.

How to apply it

  1. Set the task's permitted call allowance and record how nested operations, retries and failures consume it.
  2. Before dispatch, check the action's authorization and reserve its budget through the execution controller.
  3. Record the call identity, purpose, outcome and actual resource information that the tool exposes.
  4. Preserve the cumulative counter across handoffs and restarts, reconciling uncertain or in-flight actions conservatively.
  5. Stop before exceeding the allowance and return the best available evidence, unresolved obligation and owner decision needed.

Illustrative example

An agent has a bounded allowance for investigating and repairing one test failure. Repeated failed retrievals still consume calls, and a delegated inspection shares the same task accounting. Before starting a long test command, the controller also checks the remaining time allowance. Reaching the call cap produces a hold with the diagnostic history; it does not permit skipping required evidence to claim completion.

What to check

  • The task cannot reset its usage by restarting, spawning a worker or renaming an attempt.
  • A rejected or failed operation follows the documented accounting rule.
  • The final record separates call count from monetary cost, duration and permitted effects.

Expected outputs

  • Persistent per-task call ledger and remaining allowance.
  • Budget-stop record with completed evidence and unresolved work.

Risks and failure modes

  • A restrictive counter can encourage oversized calls or hide many actions inside one tool invocation.
  • Counting only successful calls can reward uncontrolled retries and understate the work actually consumed.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality
