PAT:022PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Trust Calibration

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Compare expressed confidence or reliance with independently assessed performance in a defined task class, then adjust how recommendations are used. Make evidence and uncertainty visible before the acceptance decision. Trust calibration is an evaluation and decision practice; a persuasive tone, a second agreeing model or a label such as high confidence does not establish calibrated correctness.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Help reviewers rely on useful assistance without confusing fluency, familiarity or model agreement with evidence of correctness.

When to use it

  • AI-generated findings influence whether reviewers investigate, accept or dismiss a candidate.
  • A team wants to understand when its confidence in a tool matches observed results.

When to avoid it

  • There is no independent outcome assessment against which confidence can be compared.
  • A confidence label would bypass required evidence or the responsible owner's decision.

Before you start

  • A defined unit of assessment, such as a review finding or behavior prediction.
  • Independent outcome criteria and a record of confidence or reliance before the result is known.

How to apply it

  1. Specify the claim being assessed and what would count as correct, incorrect or unresolved in the relevant setting.
  2. Record the recommendation, its evidence and uncertainty before inspecting the independent outcome, avoiding retrospective confidence labels.
  3. Evaluate the outcome using sources or checks that do not merely repeat the recommendation's assumptions.
  4. Compare confidence and actual results by meaningful task or risk group, retaining false positives, misses and unresolved cases.
  5. Adjust review routing or presentation from the observed mismatch, then reassess when the tool, task mix or evidence changes.

Illustrative example

A team records whether reviewers initially rate a model's defect claims as strong, tentative or unsupported. Maintainers then investigate the claims against the code and approved behavior. Some confident claims prove false and some tentative ones reveal real defects. The team changes how evidence is shown and tracks later decisions; it does not turn those observations into a universal accuracy rating for the model.

What to check

  • Confidence or reliance is recorded before outcomes and linked to a clearly defined claim.
  • Outcome assessment is independent enough to expose confident errors rather than rubber-stamp recommendations.
  • Reported conclusions state the task scope, unresolved cases and consequences of mistaken reliance.

Expected outputs

  • Confidence-versus-outcome record with task and evidence context.
  • Revised review guidance and a trigger for renewed assessment.

Risks and failure modes

  • Selective investigation of only confident findings can bias the apparent performance.
  • A numerical score can appear calibrated while hiding a dangerous error in a rare but consequential category.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:010 · Inference-Healed Code Review
  • PAT:052 · Review Gauntlet
  • PAT:075 · Convergence Review

Suggested companion techniques for comparison or combination; these links do not assert validated effectiveness.

PAT:023PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The External Bash Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use an external shell-driven controller as one possible implementation of a bounded propose, act and observe loop. The controller maintains explicit task state, enforces permissions and budgets, and interprets typed results before another attempt. This optional companion variant describes responsibilities; it is not a production-ready Bash script or a guarantee that shell orchestration is adequate for every environment.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make repetition controlled by an inspectable process instead of allowing an agent's completion text to determine whether it runs forever.

When to use it

  • A local task has simple stages whose exit conditions and artifacts can be interpreted reliably.
  • A team can evaluate whether an external controller is a sufficient and maintainable implementation route.

When to avoid it

  • The workflow needs complex concurrent recovery or external effects that the proposed controller cannot enforce safely.
  • A loop would parse free-form model text as commands or as acceptance authority.

Before you start

  • Structured task state and result statuses with persistent accounting.
  • A restricted execution environment, controlled command construction and an owner for failure recovery.

How to apply it

  1. Define the input revision, permitted operations, protected artifacts and typed exits before implementing repetition.
  2. Run one bounded attempt and collect its candidate, diagnostic, usage and outcome through a documented interface.
  3. Persist the result and remaining budget before deciding whether another attempt is eligible.
  4. Retry only for a concrete in-scope diagnostic; route ambiguity, denied authority or unsupported state to the relevant owner.
  5. Test interruption, malformed output, command failure and exhausted budget, then stop at review readiness rather than implicit acceptance.

Illustrative example

A local controller asks an agent to repair one failing example and expects a result file naming the candidate and check outcome. When the process exits without that file, the controller records an interrupted attempt and does not treat terminal text saying done as success. A later retry uses the remaining allowance and the same protected expectation; a reviewer still decides whether the candidate is acceptable.

What to check

  • Free-form output cannot become an unchecked shell command or a success transition.
  • Restarts, failed commands and malformed results preserve state and cumulative usage.
  • The controller's stop conditions can be demonstrated independently of a cooperative model response.

Expected outputs

  • Controller interface, explicit state transitions and tested failure behavior.
  • Per-attempt evidence with a final review, hold or failure status.

Risks and failure modes

  • Fragile parsing and quoting can turn ordinary model text or filenames into unintended operations.
  • A wrapper can give a false sense of control when the invoked tool retains broader permissions than the wrapper checks.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:026 · Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality

PAT:024PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The Stop-Hook Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use a stop hook to inspect an agent's proposed exit and decide whether the current task has eligible next work. The hook consults durable state, evidence and remaining budget; it can allow a stop, return a bounded diagnostic or require escalation. Re-entry continues the same contract and accounting rather than granting a fresh objective or unlimited retries.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid premature completion claims while retaining an explicit way to stop when further autonomous work is unjustified.

When to use it

  • An existing agent runtime provides a reliable exit callback and the task has machine-checkable completion prerequisites.
  • A bounded diagnostic can legitimately guide one more attempt under the same objective.

When to avoid it

  • The hook rejects every stop until the agent asserts success more convincingly.
  • A missing owner decision or permission is being treated as something another generation attempt can resolve.

Before you start

  • An understood runtime hook contract and a durable task ledger.
  • Protected expectations plus explicit retry, hold, cancellation and review-readiness outcomes.

How to apply it

  1. Define which evidence must be present for the proposed exit and which gaps require an owner rather than another attempt.
  2. At the hook, read the exact candidate state and cumulative budget instead of relying on a prose completion summary.
  3. If an in-scope diagnostic remains and budget permits, return one bounded instruction identifying the failed obligation.
  4. Preserve the same contract and oracle on re-entry, recording the hook decision and charging all work to the existing task.
  5. Allow a typed stop for exhaustion, cancellation, unclear intention or unavailable authority, retaining the unfinished obligations for handoff.

Illustrative example

An agent proposes to stop after changing a replay function. The hook finds that its required independent replay result is missing and requests that check within the remaining budget. The check reveals an unresolved policy question, so the next hook decision is a hold for the policy owner. It does not force the agent to rewrite the expected result until the exit appears green.

What to check

  • Each re-entry has a recorded diagnostic, eligibility decision and remaining allowance.
  • Cancellation and exhausted-budget exits are possible even when the task is incomplete.
  • The hook cannot modify protected expectations or convert a review-ready state into acceptance.

Expected outputs

  • Hook decision log and persistent continuation state.
  • Current candidate evidence or a clear hold with the required owner decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • Repeated automatic re-entry can conceal a loop with no new information.
  • A runtime-specific hook may miss alternate termination paths unless those paths are explicitly tested.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:025PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

The Editor-Native Manual Loop

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Use a human-guided editor session as a complete and legitimate execution route: select one scoped action, inspect its result, obtain relevant evidence and decide what happens next. The engineer controls progression while the assistant contributes drafts, explanations or diagnostics. Manual guidance is suitable when its observed overhead is lower than maintaining an additional autonomous controller.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep simple or judgment-heavy changes manageable without adding coordination machinery that does not resolve a concrete uncertainty.

When to use it

  • A small change has a clear diff and a direct verification step.
  • Frequent interpretation decisions make interactive guidance useful and affordable.

When to avoid it

  • A long task loses critical state whenever the editor session closes.
  • The engineer is expected to rubber-stamp every tool action without inspecting the consequential decisions.

Before you start

  • A clear authorized objective and the existing repository permission boundaries.
  • A practical way to inspect the diff, run relevant checks and retain the final decision.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the next meaningful increment and identify what the assistant may inspect or change.
  2. Ask for a candidate or diagnostic with its assumptions visible, keeping the approved behavior separate from the proposed implementation.
  3. Inspect the changed code or artifact and run the check appropriate to its actual consequence.
  4. Use the observation to continue, revise the approach or stop for clarification; do not repeat suggestions without a new reason.
  5. Retain a short record of the final revision, evidence, unresolved issues and responsible acceptance decision.

Illustrative example

A maintainer corrects a non-authoritative help heading with assistance in the editor. They inspect the one-file diff and render the page to confirm its appearance and links. No parallel coordinator is needed. If the edit unexpectedly changes executable routing text, they pause to clarify the newly affected behavior instead of assuming the same lightweight route remains adequate.

What to check

  • The final diff stays within the agreed scope or records an authorized change to it.
  • The check answers the actual obligation, such as rendered wording or runtime behavior, rather than merely confirming that the file saved.
  • The maintainer can explain the result and what would require a stronger review route.

Expected outputs

  • Scoped candidate with proportionate verification evidence.
  • Short decision record and any trigger for reconsidering the execution route.

Risks and failure modes

  • Interactive convenience can make unrecorded assumptions difficult to recover later.
  • A confident human can still accept a plausible generated change without checking its consequential behavior.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:001 · Plan-Then-Execute
  • PAT:046 · Small Verifiable Chunks
  • PAT:048 · The Explainability Test

PAT:026PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Retry a bounded task only when a concrete observation provides a reason to expect the next attempt to address an identified failure. Preserve the authorized objective and protected expectations, record the attempted remedy and recheck the candidate. Done means reaching the appropriate reviewed state or a named stop, not an assumption that enough retries must eventually converge.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Replace indefinite regeneration with a sequence of explainable repairs whose eligibility can be checked by someone outside the maker.

When to use it

  • A test, reproduction or concrete review finding identifies an in-scope defect.
  • The next attempt has a plausible targeted remedy and sufficient remaining budget.

When to avoid it

  • The only feedback is that the answer is unsatisfactory, with no actionable observation.
  • The disagreement concerns intended behavior, unavailable authority or a prohibited operation.

Before you start

  • A persistent task and attempt record with explicit budgets and exits.
  • An oracle or other evidence source that the maker cannot rewrite to achieve a pass.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the failed obligation, exact candidate, diagnostic and relevant environment before proposing another attempt.
  2. Decide whether the failure is repairable within the current contract or needs a named owner to clarify scope.
  3. State the narrow change expected to address the diagnostic and check that it is permitted and affordable.
  4. Apply the repair, rerun the protected check and examine relevant regressions for unintended effects.
  5. Continue only if new evidence supports another eligible attempt; otherwise retain the history and stop as review-ready, exhausted, blocked or escalated.

Illustrative example

A checker shows that a revised export drops one allowed status value. The maker corrects that mapping and reruns the status cases. The next review raises an unresolved question about whether that status should exist for a different customer class. This is no longer a mechanical retry: the task stops for a requirement decision, preserving the previous failure and the repaired candidate.

What to check

  • Each retry names both the prior diagnostic and the remedy it is testing.
  • The objective, protected expectation and cumulative budget remain intact across attempts.
  • The exit explains whether evidence is sufficient for review or which unresolved issue prevents further action.

Expected outputs

  • Attempt ledger linking diagnostics, remedies, candidates and results.
  • Review-ready evidence or an explicit stop with the required next decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • An agent can overfit a visible failure while missing adjacent behavior.
  • Repeated rejection without useful diagnostics can consume resources and encourage unauthorized changes to the success criterion.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:027PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Separate the responsibility for producing a candidate from the responsibility for checking its claims, while protecting the approved objective and expected results from both inappropriate edits and self-approval. Evaluate independence through the origin of expectations, available evidence and effective permissions. Two roles or two models can still share the same mistake and cannot replace accountable acceptance.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Give a candidate a meaningful opportunity to fail against evidence the maker did not define merely by observing its own output.

When to use it

  • A wrong-but-green candidate would have a material consequence or be difficult for a reviewer to spot.
  • The workflow can separate candidate production, independent findings and final acceptance authority.

When to avoid it

  • The checker simply repeats the maker's explanation or uses expectations generated from the candidate.
  • A second role adds ceremony while the maker can still rewrite the protected oracle.

Before you start

  • Expected behavior derived from an authorized source with a protected revision.
  • Distinct effective permissions and result channels for maker, checker and acceptance owner.

How to apply it

  1. Define what the maker may change and exclude the approved contract and protected expected results from its write scope.
  2. Give the checker the actual candidate, relevant authority and independently justified cases rather than only the maker's summary.
  3. Have the checker seek discrepancies and report reproducible findings with locators, assumptions and uncertainty.
  4. Return confirmed in-scope failures as bounded repair requests; send ambiguous requirements to their owner.
  5. Present the renewed candidate and current evidence to the accountable reviewer, preserving the distinction between checked and accepted.

Illustrative example

The maker changes how stored decisions replay. A checker runs an independently specified case requiring the original response to survive a policy update. It reports a concrete mismatch but cannot edit the candidate. The maker repairs the implementation without changing that expectation. The final reviewer inspects current results and decides whether the candidate can advance; no checker status alone grants release approval.

What to check

  • The expected answer has an origin independent of the candidate's observed output.
  • Neither role can silently alter protected authority or convert its own claim into acceptance.
  • A known wrong candidate is rejected, and evidence is renewed after a relevant repair.

Expected outputs

  • Role and permission map plus independently grounded findings.
  • Candidate-bound evidence and a separate acceptance disposition.

Risks and failure modes

  • Different model names can mask shared context gaps or the same faulty requirement.
  • A read-only checker cannot protect an expectation that the maker remains able to edit.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:028PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Skills and Context Engineering: Remove Intent Debt

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Package recurring work instructions as a maintained, versioned skill or context aid with an owner, applicability and source references. Separate procedural guidance from retrieved evidence, task state and tool permissions. The aim is to make missing or ambiguous intent visible and reduce repeated clarification where justified, without claiming that a larger instruction file removes all intent debt.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make recurring procedural knowledge reusable while preserving a clear path to the current authorized objective and its unresolved questions.

When to use it

  • A repeated task has stable procedural steps that workers otherwise reconstruct inconsistently.
  • Recurring misunderstandings can be traced to omitted context or unclear precedence.

When to avoid it

  • A one-off instruction would be generalized without evidence of reuse.
  • The proposed skill mixes tool credentials, authority decisions and unverified repository claims into one trusted block.

Before you start

  • A named maintainer and a versioned source for the procedure.
  • Applicability conditions, required inputs, expected outputs and independently enforced permission boundaries.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the recurring failure and write only the procedural guidance needed to address it.
  2. State scope, input requirements, evidence requirements and stop conditions, linking authoritative sources instead of copying mutable rules everywhere.
  3. Version and review the guidance, separating stable instructions from task-specific state and retrieved material.
  4. At use time, verify applicability and freshness against the current task and permissions; keep unresolved intent visible.
  5. Record concrete failures or maintenance changes, then revise or retire the skill when it no longer provides useful guidance.

Illustrative example

A team writes a release-note drafting skill that requires a defined revision range, source links and explicit exclusions. The skill explains the workflow but grants no publishing access and contains no permanent claim about which features are released. Each run obtains its current approved inputs. When the release process changes, the owner updates the version and records which old instructions should no longer be used.

What to check

  • The skill identifies its owner, version, applicable tasks and renewal triggers.
  • A worker can distinguish procedural advice from evidence and authoritative decisions.
  • A useful trial checks the actual deliverable and exposes missing context rather than merely confirming the skill file was loaded.

Expected outputs

  • Versioned, owned procedural guidance with source links.
  • Applicability and renewal record from actual uses.

Risks and failure modes

  • Accumulated instructions can conflict or crowd out the evidence needed for the present task.
  • An apparently official skill can launder an old assumption into a current requirement unless its authority and scope are checked.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:007 · Compounding Engineering

PAT:029PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Memory and Retrieval: Read What the Model Could Not Know

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Retrieve task-relevant information that is absent from the model's immediate context, preserving source, revision, validity and authority. Memory can contain past actions, semantic summaries, instructions or approved decisions, and those types are not interchangeable. A useful system can abstain when evidence is missing or conflicting instead of turning retrieved plausibility into approved knowledge.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Ground a task in the information it actually needs while keeping uncertainty and conflicting sources available for review.

When to use it

  • Repository-specific decisions, recent changes or task history are needed to answer the next question.
  • A long-running task needs selective access to evidence beyond a compact resume record.

When to avoid it

  • The system treats the top-ranked passage as authoritative without checking its provenance.
  • A missing decision is being filled by a plausible historical analogy instead of being raised with its owner.

Before you start

  • Source records with stable locators, revisions and validity scopes.
  • A distinction between instructions, evidence, task state and authoritative decisions.

How to apply it

  1. Define the information need and the type of claim required: observation, current rule, past event or procedural instruction.
  2. Retrieve candidate sources and retain their identities, scope and dates or versions relevant to the task.
  3. Check applicability and authority, consulting original records when a derived summary cannot resolve a consequential claim.
  4. Present supported facts separately from inferences, conflicts and omissions; abstain on unresolved questions that affect acceptance.
  5. Bind useful retrieved evidence to the task record and set renewal triggers for any derived memory reused later.

Illustrative example

A resumed agent finds two cards describing different policy thresholds. It checks the source revisions and discovers that one governs historical decisions while the other governs new requests. It retrieves the approved delta and preserves both scoped facts. If the relevant approval record is unavailable, it reports that gap instead of choosing the newer-looking card as authority.

What to check

  • Material claims can be traced from a summary back to the source used.
  • Current applicability and authority are checked independently of retrieval rank or recency.
  • Missing or contradictory evidence produces an explicit uncertainty or owner question rather than a fabricated answer.

Expected outputs

  • Task-specific evidence set with provenance and applicability.
  • Derived memory or answer that distinguishes supported claims, inference and unresolved gaps.

Risks and failure modes

  • Retrieved instructions embedded in untrusted material can attempt to cross the tool-permission boundary.
  • A compressed memory card may omit the qualifier that determines whether a fact applies to the present task.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:030PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Connectors and Tools: Move Exact Work Outside the Weights

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Delegate exact retrieval, computation or controlled operations to tools whose interfaces and outputs can be checked. The model selects or explains work while the executor performs the specified operation within an enforced permission envelope. Deterministic arithmetic or successful API execution establishes only that operation's result; it does not authorize the external effect or validate the task's underlying assumptions.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Move operations requiring precise execution into inspectable tools while keeping interpretation and authority decisions explicit.

When to use it

  • A task needs reproducible calculations, repository queries or structured transformations.
  • A supported connector can perform a clearly authorized operation more reliably than manual transcription.

When to avoid it

  • The requested operation or destination exceeds the task's authority.
  • The interface cannot identify what data or external resource the operation will affect.

Before you start

  • A documented input and output contract with the relevant data or resource identity.
  • An external enforcement point for access, effect scope and applicable budgets.

How to apply it

  1. Define the operation precisely, including units, source version, target resource and any side effects.
  2. Check input assumptions and authorization before dispatch; use a read-only or preview operation when that answers the task.
  3. Execute through the controlled interface and capture the actual status, output and relevant provenance.
  4. Validate the result against the expected shape and meaning, distinguishing executor errors from incorrect assumptions in the request.
  5. Use the result only for its supported purpose and require any separate authority needed for a consequential follow-on action.

Illustrative example

An agent calculates the changed and added files between two website packages using a script over file hashes. The script can determine exact byte differences for those inputs. The agent still checks that the chosen baseline is the published package. Producing a correct delta does not grant permission to upload it to the public site or to alter unrelated repository settings.

What to check

  • Inputs identify the intended source, target, units and revision unambiguously.
  • The recorded tool result concerns the operation actually requested, with failures preserved.
  • A precise output is not used to infer an approval or effect outside the operation's authority.

Expected outputs

  • Structured operation record with inputs, output and source identity.
  • Validated result and any separate decision required for its use.

Risks and failure modes

  • A broadly scoped connector can turn a small interpretation error into a consequential external write.
  • Silent coercion, stale resource selection or missing units can produce a precise but misleading result.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:031PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Worktrees: Isolate the Write Domains

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Use separate worktrees or equivalent isolated checkouts so concurrent workers produce changes in distinct write domains. Tie each workspace to an input revision and a named task, then integrate deliberately with fresh evidence. Filesystem separation prevents some edit collisions, but ownership of the logical outcome and shared external resources still require explicit coordination.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep concurrent candidate changes inspectable and recoverable until a designated integration point reconciles them.

When to use it

  • Independent implementation tasks can proceed without sharing mutable working files.
  • Alternative candidates need to be compared against the same baseline before selecting one.

When to avoid it

  • Workers require concurrent uncoordinated access to one shared database or authoritative artifact.
  • Creating separate directories is being treated as sufficient protection against overlapping logical responsibilities.

Before you start

  • A baseline revision and an ownership map for logical targets.
  • A named integrator and controls for shared resources outside the working directories.

How to apply it

  1. Assign a unique task and target to each workspace, recording the baseline and permitted write scope.
  2. Create or select the isolated checkout and verify its state before work begins, preserving any existing user work.
  3. Keep candidate artifacts and checks associated with their workspace and revision rather than a shared mutable status file.
  4. Review dependencies and integrate selected changes through the owner, resolving semantic conflicts as well as textual conflicts.
  5. Renew relevant checks on the integrated candidate and retire workspaces only after required artifacts and unresolved work are accounted for.

Illustrative example

One worker updates export documentation while another repairs an independent parser test in a separate checkout. The coordinator discovers that both also propose renaming the same public option. That logical overlap is resolved by assigning one owner, even though the files were edited in isolation. After integration, the combined documentation and behavior checks run against the resulting revision.

What to check

  • Each workspace has the expected baseline, owner and allowed target.
  • The coordinator detects duplicate logical changes and shared-resource dependencies before integration.
  • The accepted evidence belongs to the integrated candidate, including any resolution of conflicts.

Expected outputs

  • Workspace-to-task map with isolated candidate artifacts.
  • Integration record, renewed checks and accounted-for remaining work.

Risks and failure modes

  • Shared credentials or service endpoints can bypass the intended separation of write effects.
  • Conflict-free textual merges can still combine incompatible assumptions about behavior or interfaces.

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:032PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Assign one current owner to each logical target across concurrent loops, using bounded work concessions or leases where needed. Ownership names the task, contract revision, validity and generation so stale workers cannot submit as current. Coordination must operate above filenames and preserve decision rights, because separate files can encode the same policy or competing implementations.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent duplicate or stale work from entering integration under an apparently valid assignment.

When to use it

  • Several agents or repeated triggers can act on the same backlog item or logical component.
  • A task can outlive its original contract revision, assignment or coordinator session.

When to avoid it

  • No shared mutable or duplicate target exists and a lease system would add needless complexity.
  • A local example is assumed to provide race-safe distributed ownership without further implementation.

Before you start

  • Canonical target identities and a coordinator able to grant, renew and revoke assignments.
  • A state record containing owner, task, contract revision, expiry and assignment generation.

How to apply it

  1. Define logical targets so semantically overlapping changes cannot evade ownership by touching different files.
  2. Grant a bounded assignment only when the target is available and its prerequisites and review capacity are satisfied.
  3. Require progress and submissions to carry the current assignment identity, intention revision and candidate evidence.
  4. On expiry, cancellation or changed intention, invalidate affected concessions and preserve prior work as historical or pending reconciliation.
  5. Accept a submission for review only after checking its current assignment and evidence, then release or explicitly transfer ownership.

Illustrative example

A worker receives the task of updating a pricing rule, while another investigates its documentation. The policy revision changes before the first worker submits. Its old assignment and green tests are retained but rejected as current evidence. The coordinator grants a new generation after the owner resolves the change, preventing the delayed old submission from overwriting the newly assigned work.

What to check

  • Competing requests for the same logical target cannot both obtain current ownership under the implemented model.
  • Stale generations, expired leases and duplicate event identities have explicit outcomes.
  • Submission checks use current authority and evidence, not only the state recorded when work started.

Expected outputs

  • Target ownership and concession history with explicit invalidations.
  • Current submissions, rejected stale events and unresolved integration decisions.

Risks and failure modes

  • Clock assumptions, race conditions or coordinator failures can undermine a naive lease implementation.
  • A poorly defined target map can allow two owners to change the same business rule through different artifacts.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:033PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Budget and Observability: Price the Next Attempt

Family. Economics, Infrastructure and Work

Before another attempt, estimate its incremental burden and compare that decision with the cumulative task record. Include setup, generation, tools, verification, review, waiting and rejected work without double-counting. Use observations where available and label uncertain inputs. A cheap next call may still be a poor choice when checking capacity, authority or the probability of useful progress is missing.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make continuation an explicit engineering and economic decision while preserving required controls as eligibility conditions.

When to use it

  • A loop can spend more time or resources on repeated attempts, extra agents or another review stage.
  • A team compares candidate execution routes for the same class of accepted changes.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed saving comes from omitting a required permission or independent check.
  • Only inference cost is available but the result is presented as total delivery cost.

Before you start

  • A task ledger with stable event identities and distinct cost or time categories.
  • An eligible next action and explicit assumptions for unobserved costs or outcomes.

How to apply it

  1. Record costs already incurred, including failed attempts and initial setup, with observed and estimated values distinguishable.
  2. Identify the next permitted action and the diagnostic or uncertainty it is expected to resolve.
  3. Estimate its marginal execution, checking, reviewer and integration burden, accounting for existing capacity constraints.
  4. Compare continuing, simplifying, using a human-led route or stopping under the same required controls.
  5. Authorize the eligible choice through the task's existing budget rules, then record the actual outcome to improve later estimates.

Illustrative example

After two unsuccessful repairs, a team considers a third model run or a short maintainer investigation. The ledger includes setup, tool use and the review already spent, while the next-step estimate separates those sunk costs from the new decision. An unresolved policy question makes another generation attempt ineligible regardless of its small token cost; the team routes the question to its owner.

What to check

  • Cumulative accounting includes abandoned and rejected work as well as accepted results.
  • Person-time, elapsed waiting and cash charges are reported distinctly before aggregation.
  • The chosen action has both a valid permission path and a plausible information benefit under stated assumptions.

Expected outputs

  • Task cost ledger and next-action decision with assumptions.
  • Observed outcome, remaining budget and any revised continuation threshold.

Risks and failure modes

  • Ignoring review and integration can make a low-cost producer appear efficient while total accepted-change cost rises.
  • A precise spreadsheet can hide uncertainty about acceptance, correlated retries or rare consequential failures.

PAT:034PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Safety and Guardrails: Verification Is Not Authorization

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Keep three questions separate: whether an operation is permitted, whether its result satisfies a check, and who may accept or publish the change. Enforce the permission envelope before execution and evaluate evidence afterward. A passing test, clean scanner or policy-shaped file supplies only its specific finding; none silently grants the authority of a neighboring decision.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent technical success from being used to cross a boundary that requires a different owner's authority.

When to use it

  • A workflow passes from candidate creation through review toward a consequential external action.
  • Several checks and actors contribute evidence that could be mistaken for one combined approval.

When to avoid it

  • An established workflow already separates permissions, checks and acceptance; map the practice to those controls instead of introducing parallel approval stages.
  • A small, pre-authorized edit has a clear owner and verification path; retain that path without adding redundant decision stages.

Before you start

  • Named decision rights for scope, tool access, acceptance and any external publication or release.
  • Checks whose supported claims and unverified boundaries are explicit.

How to apply it

  1. Map the next operation to the actor, target and existing authority that would permit it.
  2. Enforce that permission before the tool acts, independently of the model's confidence or expected result.
  3. Run the relevant checks and record their actual scope, candidate revision and limitations.
  4. Present the evidence to the role responsible for the next decision, preserving any missing authority or unresolved risk.
  5. Record that decision separately and recheck applicability if the candidate, contract, destination or permissions change.

Illustrative example

An agent creates a patch that passes functional tests and a dependency scan. Those findings support review of the candidate, but the task only authorizes local preparation. The release owner still decides deployment through the established process. Conversely, an owner may authorize a release review, but that permission cannot be described as evidence that an unrun security check passed.

What to check

  • No successful test or scanner result changes the execution permission profile.
  • The acceptance or publication decision identifies the responsible authority and the exact eligible candidate.
  • Missing evidence and missing authorization remain distinguishable in the final status.

Expected outputs

  • Decision-rights map and enforced operation outcomes.
  • Candidate evidence plus a separate, scoped decision record.

Risks and failure modes

  • Combining all statuses into one green indicator can conceal which obligation remains unmet.
  • Repository text or generated metadata can impersonate an approval unless the real identity and authority path are checked.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:035PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Daily Triage: rank the rare urgent item

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Use a bounded triage pass to identify a small set of potentially urgent items from a larger stream, showing the evidence and uncertainty behind their proposed order. Preserve deferred work and route consequential cases to the right owner. This optional companion workflow proposes priorities; ranking an issue does not authorize a fix, a policy change or a message to an external party.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Focus limited human attention on items whose delay may matter, without converting automated ranking into unattended execution.

When to use it

  • A queue is large enough that manually scanning every item repeatedly imposes a real burden.
  • The team can state what makes an item urgent and who decides its disposition.

When to avoid it

  • The ranking would automatically trigger consequential actions without the queue owner's decision.
  • Available item descriptions omit the evidence needed to distinguish urgency from confident wording.

Before you start

  • A bounded source queue and explicit priority or escalation criteria.
  • A named triage owner with capacity to examine the proposed urgent set and a record of deferred items.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the queue snapshot and the time window, preserving item identity and current status.
  2. Apply the stated criteria using linked evidence, separating urgency, impact, uncertainty and age where they mean different things.
  3. Produce a small ranked proposal with reasons, missing information and any rule-based mandatory escalation.
  4. Have the owner review uncertain or consequential cases and record a disposition without silently dropping the rest.
  5. Review outcomes later, including missed urgent items and false alarms, and adjust the triage criteria or assistance only from those observations.

Illustrative example

A daily repository queue contains many documentation suggestions and one report of changed replay behavior. The assistant flags the replay report because its linked reproduction may violate a protected invariant, while labeling the evidence incomplete. The owner checks the report and assigns the next action. The assistant's ranking does not permit it to change the replay policy or contact affected customers.

What to check

  • Each proposed urgent item has a traceable reason tied to the stated criteria.
  • Deferred and unassessed items remain visible, including relevant ageing or follow-up needs.
  • Evaluation counts false alarms and missed urgent cases rather than only correct top-ranked suggestions.

Expected outputs

  • Ranked triage proposal with evidence, uncertainties and retained backlog.
  • Owner dispositions and later outcome observations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Overfitting the criteria to common items can hide the rare event the process was meant to surface.
  • Automated urgency labels can consume scarce review capacity and displace quieter but consequential work.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:036PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

CI Sweeper: classify before fixing

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Inspect failed continuous-integration work and classify the evidence before deciding whether a code repair is warranted. Distinguish a candidate regression, known baseline failure, environmental problem, potentially intermittent behavior and unresolved cause. The optional sweeper creates a routed diagnostic or bounded repair proposal; it does not infer that every red build is a software defect the agent may fix.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Reduce indiscriminate CI repair by making the failure type, candidate identity and appropriate owner explicit first.

When to use it

  • Many failed jobs require initial diagnosis before maintainers can assign work.
  • The same repository has both candidate regressions and infrastructure or pre-existing failures.

When to avoid it

  • The workflow reruns jobs until green and discards the failed observations.
  • The proposed repair crosses the current task scope or weakens a required check.

Before you start

  • Job logs, exact candidate and baseline identities, and relevant environment information.
  • An agreed classification vocabulary that permits unknown and an owner for each route.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the failure signature, command, revision, timing and environment details before logs expire or another run replaces them.
  2. Compare the failure with the baseline and available related runs, avoiding claims unsupported by missing history.
  3. Classify the evidence with a confidence boundary and list the observation needed to resolve competing explanations.
  4. For a reproducible in-scope regression, create a bounded repair request; otherwise route the diagnostic to the appropriate maintainer or infrastructure owner.
  5. Retain reruns and final dispositions so later success does not erase the original failure or create a false causal explanation.

Illustrative example

A build fails during package retrieval before any changed code runs. A later rerun succeeds. The sweeper records an environmental candidate explanation and the two run identities, but does not declare the test flaky or alter source code. Another failure reproduces on the patch and not the baseline, providing a stronger basis for a focused repair proposal to the component owner.

What to check

  • A classification is supported by actual runs and clearly separates observations from inferred causes.
  • A passing rerun does not delete the failure or automatically satisfy policies requiring investigation.
  • Any proposed repair has a relevant owner, bounded scope and evidence that distinguishes it from unrelated work.

Expected outputs

  • Failure classification with diagnostic evidence and unresolved hypotheses.
  • Routed owner decision or scoped repair proposal with retained run history.

Risks and failure modes

  • Grouping failures by similar log text can combine unrelated causes.
  • Repeated reruns can hide an unstable environment and consume capacity without yielding a useful diagnosis.

PAT:037PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Dependency Sweeper: route by risk

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Route dependency updates according to their specific compatibility, provenance and effect risks instead of treating all version changes alike. Establish the package identity and proposed change, inspect relevant evidence, and create a proportionate review path. This optional maintenance workflow produces a candidate and risk record; passing CI does not authorize a dependency's adoption, its permissions or the merge.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make dependency maintenance reviewable by connecting each proposed update to the behavior, trust boundary and owner it affects.

When to use it

  • A repository has recurring dependency updates that require different levels of investigation.
  • A maintainer needs to separate routine candidates from updates changing interfaces, build behavior or execution privileges.

When to avoid it

  • Package identity or provenance is uncertain and the proposed automation would install first and investigate later.
  • The route assumes every patch-level version is harmless or every passing update may merge unattended.

Before you start

  • A known dependency baseline, lock or resolution record, and authorized update scope.
  • A dependency owner and access to relevant upstream or repository evidence.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the exact package, source, resolved version and proposed version, including transitive changes that affect the candidate.
  2. Review relevant compatibility notes, provenance and build or runtime effects, retaining unknowns rather than inventing reassurance.
  3. Route the candidate by the actual affected boundaries and project rules, assigning specialist review when justified.
  4. Prepare the bounded update and run checks relevant to its use, including behavior that may not be covered by installation success.
  5. Present the changed resolution, evidence and residual uncertainty for the authorized adoption and integration decision.

Illustrative example

A dependency update changes only a declared version in the manifest but also changes the resolved parser used by the application. The sweeper records that transitive difference and proposes compatibility cases for the input formats the service supports. Even if those cases pass, the maintainer still assesses package provenance and the project-specific approval path before accepting the update.

What to check

  • The candidate's actual resolution matches the package identities and versions in the review record.
  • Checks cover the dependency's consequential local use rather than merely a successful install.
  • Unknown provenance, new privileges or compatibility gaps remain visible to the responsible approver.

Expected outputs

  • Dependency change inventory and evidence-based routing decision.
  • Bounded update candidate with checks, owner and residual risks.

Risks and failure modes

  • A harmless-looking top-level update can alter transitive code or installation behavior.
  • Treating vulnerability scanning as a complete safety verdict can miss provenance, licensing or operational questions outside its scope.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:038PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Duplicate detection

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Use retrieval or similarity analysis to propose records that may describe the same underlying issue, practice or change, then confirm the semantic relationship before consolidation. Preserve stable identifiers, source evidence and historical dispositions. A duplicate candidate may instead be a related topic, a recurrence, a different affected version or a distinct request with similar wording.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Reduce repeated investigation while retaining distinctions needed for ownership, version history and accountable decisions.

When to use it

  • A catalogue or issue queue contains repeated titles, paraphrases or overlapping reports.
  • Maintainers need to locate prior work before deciding whether a new item is genuinely redundant.

When to avoid it

  • The source records lack enough evidence to determine whether they concern the same behavior.
  • The process would delete or close items automatically based only on textual similarity.

Before you start

  • Stable record identifiers with source links, affected versions and current status.
  • A responsible reviewer and a way to represent related, duplicate, recurring and unresolved relationships.

How to apply it

  1. Retrieve candidate pairs or groups using labels, content and relevant metadata, retaining the basis for the suggestion.
  2. Compare the underlying outcome, affected component, version, reproduction and requested action rather than the title alone.
  3. Classify the relationship explicitly and identify any uncertainty that needs the record owner.
  4. If consolidation is justified, choose a canonical navigation target while preserving every original record and its provenance.
  5. Link the records and retain their historical dispositions, ensuring searches can still discover aliases and explain the consolidation.

Illustrative example

Two issue titles both say export order is unstable. One concerns the current CSV endpoint; the other concerns historical PDF reports and has a different reproduction. The system proposes them as similar, but the maintainer marks them related rather than duplicate. Two genuinely identical reports can point to one investigation while their original reporters' evidence and affected revisions remain intact.

What to check

  • Each duplicate decision states the shared underlying behavior and the evidence supporting identity.
  • Canonical navigation preserves original identifiers, provenance and any version-specific exceptions.
  • A review sample checks false merges and missed duplicates, including records with misleadingly similar titles.

Expected outputs

  • Candidate duplicate report and reviewed relationship decisions.
  • Canonical links or aliases with preserved original history.

Risks and failure modes

  • Collapsing separate incidents can hide repeated failures that should inform maintenance priorities.
  • Retaining only the most complete-looking record can discard a counterexample that changes the diagnosis.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:039PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

PR babysitter

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Monitor a pull request's current candidate, required checks, review findings and unresolved dependencies to propose its next action. Bind every readiness claim to the exact revision and relevant authority. This optional companion workflow helps maintainers follow evidence as a PR changes; it must distinguish a truly eligible review candidate from a false-ready status based on stale or incomplete information.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Reduce forgotten review obligations without replacing the maintainer's decision with an automated status summary.

When to use it

  • Pull requests wait across multiple revisions, checks and reviewer exchanges.
  • Maintainers need a compact view of what specifically blocks the next legitimate stage.

When to avoid it

  • The monitor would merge because checks appear green or comments have been answered.
  • It cannot determine whether a result or review applies to the current candidate.

Before you start

  • Access to current candidate and base identities, required checks and review dispositions.
  • A project-defined readiness policy and a named owner for exceptions or acceptance.

How to apply it

  1. Capture the current PR revision, relevant base, contract or requirement revision and mandatory evidence.
  2. Associate each check and substantive review finding with the candidate it actually concerns.
  3. Identify stale evidence, unresolved findings, missing decisions and dependency changes rather than flattening them into one status.
  4. Propose the next bounded action, such as rerunning a check, requesting a clarification or presenting a current bundle to the reviewer.
  5. Recompute readiness after changes and retain false-ready incidents as an explicit outcome for improving the monitor.

Illustrative example

A pull request passed checks, then received a new commit adjusting replay behavior. The monitor finds that the visible approval and independent replay result concern the previous revision. It reports the precise stale evidence and prepares the current diff for review. Answering the earlier comment or seeing one green job does not restore readiness until the applicable evidence is renewed under the repository's policy.

What to check

  • Every required result and review disposition matches the revision or supported scope claimed.
  • A newly pushed commit or relevant base change invalidates only the evidence whose applicability must be renewed.
  • The monitor can demonstrate a false-ready case and reports it separately from ordinary waiting.

Expected outputs

  • Revision-specific readiness report with blockers and next actions.
  • Evidence renewal and disposition history, including false-ready observations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Automated reminders can add noise or pressure without resolving the actual missing decision.
  • A stale approval can look authoritative when its associated candidate identity is hidden.

PAT:040PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Post-merge cleanup

Family. Architecture, Evolution and Maintenance

Inspect the integrated result for justified follow-up maintenance, such as obsolete temporary artifacts, duplicated explanations or incomplete handoff notes. Produce scoped proposals with evidence and ownership before making further changes. Merge is a new baseline for inspection, not standing permission for broad cleanup or proof that every leftover item is safe to remove.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep integration from leaving avoidable maintenance burden while preserving the obligations and history needed by the next engineer.

When to use it

  • A completed change leaves known temporary scaffolding or an explicitly deferred maintenance item.
  • Integration reveals duplicated or outdated material that a maintainer should assess.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed cleanup has no demonstrated consequence beyond aesthetic preference.
  • Deletion could remove user work, recovery evidence or a consumer whose existence has not been checked.

Before you start

  • An identified integrated baseline and the original task's actual cleanup authorization.
  • An owner for each affected target and evidence of the artifact's current purpose or obsolescence.

How to apply it

  1. Inspect the integrated diff and deferred-work record for specific follow-up candidates rather than scanning for unrestricted rewrites.
  2. For each candidate, identify its purpose, consumers, retention needs and the consequence of leaving or changing it.
  3. Separate cleanup already authorized by the task from new maintenance proposals that need their own scope decision.
  4. Apply eligible changes in a bounded candidate and verify the relevant behavior, documentation or recovery path.
  5. Record the outcome and preserve the rationale for retained items or deferred proposals so a later sweeper does not rediscover the same uncertainty.

Illustrative example

After an API migration merges, a temporary compatibility note appears outdated. The maintainer checks that the old endpoint still serves one documented client, so the note remains with a revised validity statement. An unused migration scratch file can be removed within the authorized cleanup scope. A broader rewrite of the adapter becomes a separate proposal with its own behavior and review requirements.

What to check

  • Each removal or rewrite has evidence about its purpose and affected consumers.
  • The candidate stays within explicit cleanup authority and preserves required historical or recovery artifacts.
  • Relevant checks run on the integrated baseline rather than an obsolete pre-merge workspace.

Expected outputs

  • Scoped maintenance proposal or authorized cleanup candidate.
  • Verified result and rationale for items retained, changed or deferred.

Risks and failure modes

  • Broad cleanup can obscure the original change and create unrelated regressions.
  • Deleting evidence too early can make later diagnosis or rollback reasoning harder even when the running code is unaffected.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Quality, Architecture and Maintainability — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:041PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Changelog drafter

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Draft a changelog from a defined change range and attributable evidence, separating implemented changes, user-visible effects, unresolved work and actual release status. Preserve links that let a reviewer challenge each material statement. The draft communicates verified scope; it is not itself proof that work completed, was accepted, reached production or produced the claimed benefit.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn a set of changes into an accurate reader-facing account without letting generated prose enlarge the delivered scope.

When to use it

  • A release or update has a clear baseline and target whose differences need explanation.
  • Maintainers need a concise draft that traces claims to the accepted change record.

When to avoid it

  • The release range or actual publication status is unknown.
  • The draft would infer user benefits or completed work from plans, commit messages or unreviewed proposals alone.

Before you start

  • Identified baseline and target revisions with relevant issue, diff and verification records.
  • An editor or release owner who can confirm the audience, terminology and publication status.

How to apply it

  1. Establish the exact comparison range and distinguish accepted changes from proposals, reverted work and unrelated commits.
  2. Inspect the actual diff and supporting records, identifying externally meaningful behavior and any compatibility or migration implications.
  3. Draft concise claims linked to their evidence, labeling unknown deployment or validation status rather than filling gaps.
  4. Have the responsible reviewer check completeness, wording, breaking effects and the relationship between code changes and actual release.
  5. Publish only through the authorized process and preserve the reviewed range and evidence links for future correction.

Illustrative example

A website update translates practice descriptions and adds a catalogue collection. The draft points to the changed catalogue data and verified navigation, while distinguishing those completed package changes from deployment to the public site. It does not say the update is live merely because a ZIP exists. A reviewer checks the range and removes a claim about unrelated articles that were not changed in this release.

What to check

  • Every material statement is supported by the selected change range and relevant evidence.
  • The text distinguishes implementation, acceptance, publication and measured outcomes where those statuses differ.
  • Known incompatibilities, required user actions and incomplete work are accurately represented.

Expected outputs

  • Reviewed changelog draft with evidence links and defined revision range.
  • Publication disposition and any unresolved wording or status questions.

Risks and failure modes

  • An attractive summary can overstate the scope by repeating a PR's original ambition.
  • Grouping changes too aggressively can hide an action users must take or an important compatibility boundary.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:042PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Capstone orchestra

Family. Economics, Infrastructure and Work

Compose several practices around one concrete capstone task only when each mechanism addresses a named uncertainty and justifies its marginal cost. Define the authorized outcome, shared evidence and decision rights before coordinating components. This retained companion concept is an integration exercise, not evidence that a large orchestration stack improves every task or that course materials establish operational results.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Assess whether the selected mechanisms work together to deliver one accountable outcome at an acceptable total burden.

When to use it

  • A learning or pilot task needs to examine interactions among scope, execution, verification, review and handoff.
  • Simpler routes have an identified limitation that an added mechanism could plausibly address.

When to avoid it

  • The objective is to demonstrate as many agents or tools as possible.
  • Course examples, completion statistics or cost inputs have not been checked but would be presented as observed results.

Before you start

  • A bounded task contract, independent outcome checks and a named integration owner.
  • A simpler eligible comparison route plus a ledger for setup, coordination, verification and review.

How to apply it

  1. State the outcome and consequential uncertainties, including the minimum controls required regardless of the chosen machinery.
  2. Assign a purpose to every proposed component and omit those that do not change a necessary decision or useful observation.
  3. Define interfaces, ownership, permission boundaries and evidence identities so one component cannot assume another's authority.
  4. Run the bounded composition, retaining failures, handoff losses, rejected work and the actual integration burden.
  5. Evaluate the accepted result and the marginal value of each mechanism, then simplify or stop where the evidence does not support keeping it.

Illustrative example

A capstone updates a small service and its documentation. The team compares an interactive route with a bounded maker and an independent checker, using the same requirements and behavior cases. It records setup, review and integration effort rather than counting generated artifacts. An additional debate agent is omitted because no unresolved decision needs it; any educational benefit is assessed separately through the learner's later independent work.

What to check

  • Every retained component has a named purpose, output and accountable integration boundary.
  • The outcome evidence concerns the integrated candidate and preserves required independence and authority.
  • Cost or learning conclusions distinguish observed pilot results, assumptions, unverified course claims and unknown follow-up.

Expected outputs

  • Composition and decision record with integrated candidate evidence.
  • Cost and learning observations, plus reasons to keep, simplify or retire mechanisms.

Risks and failure modes

  • A complex demonstration can reward visible activity while shifting the real burden into review.
  • Reusing illustrative course inputs as measurements can create a fabricated return or effectiveness claim.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Economics, Jobs, Risk and Evidence-Based Adoption — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:043PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Spec-First Generation

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Establish the intended behavior and representative scenarios before asking an assistant to generate a candidate implementation. The specification states obligations that an accountable owner has authorized; the implementation plan proposes how to satisfy them. Keep these separate so a convenient design cannot quietly redefine success.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make the acceptance question inspectable before implementation choices begin to shape the apparent requirements.

When to use it

  • A change affects observable behavior, compatibility, policy, or an interface used by others.
  • Several implementations are plausible and reviewers need a common basis for judging them.

When to avoid it

  • The purpose is still an exploratory hypothesis; first authorize a bounded experiment and label its provisional assumptions.

Before you start

  • A named owner can resolve consequential behavior questions.
  • Existing obligations, affected consumers, and authoritative scenarios are accessible.

How to apply it

  1. Describe outcomes, boundaries, exclusions, and failure behavior without prescribing unnecessary implementation details.
  2. Write ordinary, boundary, and negative scenarios; record where each expected result comes from.
  3. Resolve blocking questions with the owner and version the approved answers together with remaining explicit unknowns.
  4. Ask for an implementation plan that references the obligations; reject plan choices that silently change them.
  5. Generate within the permitted scope, then compare the candidate with the approved scenarios and required regressions.

Illustrative example

A service must preserve the response originally stored for a repeated request. The specification records the request identity, permitted payload, and expected historical response before an agent chooses a storage design. When the agent proposes reevaluating the request under current policy, the owner can identify a contract violation without debating the programming language or persistence library.

What to check

  • Each material acceptance claim traces to an authorized behavior statement.
  • The plan can change without changing the approved expected outcomes.
  • Unresolved high-consequence questions block the affected candidate rather than becoming implementation assumptions.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned behavior contract with scenarios.
  • A separately revisable implementation plan and an impact list.

Risks and failure modes

  • Copying implementation behavior into the specification can preserve an existing defect.
  • An elaborate document may hide a missing decision behind polished prose.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:044PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Test-Driven AI Development

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Write and examine tests before AI-assisted implementation, deriving expected results from an independently authorized behavior reference. Preserve the initial failing case, implement a bounded change, and rerun the relevant checks. The value comes from the quality and protection of the oracle, not merely the order in which files were created.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent a candidate and its generated tests from agreeing on the same incorrect interpretation of required behavior.

When to use it

  • A defect has a reproducible input and an authoritative expected outcome.
  • New behavior can be expressed through examples, invariants, or an established interface contract.

When to avoid it

  • Expected behavior is disputed or unavailable; clarify it before treating an assertion as an acceptance oracle.

Before you start

  • A protected expectation source and a reproducible test environment.
  • The maker cannot silently rewrite mandatory acceptance checks.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the requirement and independently derive the expected result, retaining its version and owner.
  2. Create a focused check and confirm that it fails on the relevant wrong behavior for the intended reason.
  3. Record the failure before implementation; distinguish a meaningful assertion failure from broken test setup.
  4. Let the maker implement the smallest coherent repair while retaining the approved expectation.
  5. Rerun the focused check and mandatory regressions; keep maker-written supplementary tests clearly identified.

Illustrative example

An old routing function approves a flagged request. Before repair, a reviewer derives a rejection expectation from the approved policy and records the failing case. The agent changes the routing condition. The same protected test now passes, while a nearby ordinary request remains covered. A new test that simply copies the agent’s output would not supply that independent challenge.

What to check

  • The original wrong implementation fails a named behavioral assertion.
  • The corrected candidate passes without an unapproved expectation change.
  • Boundary and regression checks cover relevant neighboring behavior, with omissions recorded.

Expected outputs

  • An independently grounded failing case and its post-change result.
  • A candidate-bound test report with oracle provenance.

Risks and failure modes

  • Tests generated from a defective implementation can encode its defect as the expected answer.
  • A maker with write access to the oracle can turn a real failure into a misleading pass.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:027 · Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance

PAT:045PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Exploratory Vibe Coding

Family. Scope, Exploration and Accountability

Use conversational generation to explore a design question in a reversible setting. State the hypothesis, permitted effects, and disposal or adoption decision before iterating. A promising prototype can reveal an interaction or feasibility issue, but becoming a maintained product requires a separate decision about ownership, evidence, and operational obligations.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Answer an uncertain design question cheaply enough to discard the experiment when its premise fails.

When to use it

  • A team is comparing interaction ideas or testing a narrow technical possibility.
  • Requirements are provisional and the artifact can remain isolated from consequential users and systems.

When to avoid it

  • The work would immediately control sensitive decisions or irreversible effects without an adequate authorized delivery path.

Before you start

  • A clear exploratory question, short time budget, and experiment owner.
  • Disposable data and an environment with bounded effects.

How to apply it

  1. Name the question the prototype should answer and what observation would make it unhelpful.
  2. Set the writable scope, permitted tools, data boundary, and stopping condition before generation.
  3. Iterate on the uncertain aspect; record assumptions and manual shortcuts as they are introduced.
  4. Exercise the relevant interaction or technical path and separate observations from guesses about broader behavior.
  5. Conclude with discard, another bounded experiment, or an explicit adoption proposal that identifies unmet engineering obligations.

Illustrative example

A team compares two ways to display policy exceptions using synthetic requests. An assistant generates both interfaces, and the owner observes whether users can distinguish historical and current decisions. The preferred sketch becomes design evidence. Before it enters the maintained service, the team must still review its data model, authorization behavior, accessibility, tests, and ongoing ownership.

What to check

  • The recorded finding answers the original exploratory question.
  • No prototype shortcut is silently represented as an approved product requirement.
  • Any proposed adoption names the missing evidence and the responsible decision maker.

Expected outputs

  • A bounded prototype and an observation log.
  • A disposal decision or scoped adoption proposal.

Risks and failure modes

  • Visual polish can encourage premature promotion and hide missing operational behavior.
  • Repeated exploratory changes can accumulate dependencies that make supposedly disposable work difficult to abandon.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • AI Changes the Unit of Software Work — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality
