PAT:070PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Gap-Closure Analysis

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Compare intended behavior, scenarios, interfaces, and implementation knowledge to identify candidate gaps and orphaned elements. Investigate each finding before deciding whether it represents missing coverage, an obsolete artifact, an intentional exclusion, or an unapproved assumption. Legacy observations help discover questions; they do not automatically become requirements that must be preserved.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn missing traceability and uncovered obligations into specific decisions instead of indiscriminately expanding the specification to match existing code.

When to use it

  • A brownfield change has undocumented outputs, unmapped scenarios, or unclear relationships between requirements and tests.
  • A new specification may omit a consumer or preserve behavior that no longer has an authorized purpose.

When to avoid it

  • The exercise would require preserving every legacy path without checking whether its behavior is intended.

Before you start

  • A canonical behavior reference and identifiable candidate artifacts.
  • An owner for disputed meaning and a scoped impact question.

How to apply it

  1. Map the changed obligations to relevant scenarios, interfaces, implementation elements, and evidence.
  2. Flag missing relationships and apparently orphaned elements with their exact locators and uncertainty.
  3. Investigate whether each finding is an omission, a historical remnant, a valid exclusion, or a defect in the mapping.
  4. Ask the appropriate owner to resolve consequential missing behavior and record any authorized delta.
  5. Add or revise the relevant scenario, artifact, or mapping and retain unresolved items with their impact and next action.

Illustrative example

An eligibility response includes a policy-version field, but the new scenarios assert only the decision label. Analysis flags the field as potentially uncovered. Inspection shows that consumers rely on it to explain historical decisions. The owner confirms the obligation, and an independent scenario now checks both values. Other unused legacy fields are investigated separately rather than copied into the contract by default.

What to check

  • Each accepted gap has a concrete obligation or decision behind it.
  • Dismissed findings retain a reason, such as an intentional exclusion or obsolete artifact.
  • Closure adds relevant evidence or traceability without silently broadening authority.

Expected outputs

  • A classified gap and orphan register.
  • Authorized resolutions and updated coverage links.

Risks and failure modes

  • Treating all unmapped code as required behavior can preserve defects and dead features.
  • False positives can consume review capacity without improving coverage of consequential outcomes.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

  • PAT:061 · Consistency Analysis Gate

PAT:071PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Ambiguity Scoring

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Use an explicit rubric to organize observations about a specification’s completeness, consistency, specificity, and testability. Keep the underlying findings visible and treat critical unresolved ambiguity as a separate blocking condition. A composite score may help prioritize examination; it does not establish correctness, authorize a requirement, or supply a validated universal readiness threshold.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a vague judgment that a specification is unclear more inspectable without replacing individual consequential findings with a number.

When to use it

  • Several draft areas need consistent review attention and their uncertainty is otherwise described only impressionistically.
  • A team wants to investigate whether a rubric could support local triage.

When to avoid it

  • A score would be used as automatic approval or as evidence that all requirements are complete.

Before you start

  • A defined rubric with observable anchors and example interpretations.
  • Separate recording of critical findings, owners, and resolution states.

How to apply it

  1. Define what each dimension means and which observable evidence supports each rating.
  2. Rate the relevant draft sections while retaining the exact gaps, contradictions, or unverifiable statements behind each score.
  3. Flag consequential unresolved questions independently of the aggregate and identify the work they block.
  4. Use the profile to prioritize clarification or review, then record whether the underlying finding was actually resolved.
  5. Before using thresholds predictively, evaluate local rating agreement and outcome relationships rather than assuming the numbers are calibrated.

Illustrative example

A draft scores well on readable structure and concrete examples, but never states whether a repeated request uses historical or current policy. The reviewer retains that question as blocking for replay work even though the overall score is high. After the owner resolves it, the record changes because an authoritative answer exists, not simply because a second model awards more points.

What to check

  • Every rating has an inspectable rationale tied to the relevant draft.
  • Critical open questions remain visible regardless of the composite score.
  • Any claim about predictive usefulness is supported by a separate evaluation.

Expected outputs

  • A diagnostic rating profile with source-linked findings.
  • A prioritized clarification list and explicit blocking conditions.

Risks and failure modes

  • Numerical precision can create confidence unsupported by the rubric’s validation.
  • Teams may optimize wording for a score while leaving the decisive uncertainty unresolved.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:072PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Handoff Chain

Family. Context, Memory and Handoffs

Transfer the minimum state a successor needs to continue work, with links to the fuller evidence record. Each handoff identifies its inputs, output state, versions, doubts, authority, resource history, and next permitted action. The recipient checks freshness and applicability before resuming; the presence of expected files alone is not evidence that a handoff is coherent.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Maintain continuity across people, agents, and sessions without letting compression erase constraints, failed attempts, or changed authority.

When to use it

  • Work spans sessions or passes between investigation, implementation, checking, and review roles.
  • A successor must continue from a checkpoint without replaying the entire conversation.

When to avoid it

  • The transfer would conceal that the current contract or permission state cannot be verified; stop and reconcile first.

Before you start

  • Identifiable task, candidate, contract, and evidence versions.
  • A recipient with a defined role and access to the permitted source record.

How to apply it

  1. State the current objective, completed work, candidate revision, and unresolved result in a concise structured record.
  2. Link the authoritative contract, relevant observations, failed attempts, and decision rationale rather than copying only conclusions.
  3. Carry forward consumed budget, permission scope, pending questions, and the specific next action or stopping condition.
  4. Have the recipient compare stored versions with current authority and check that referenced evidence actually applies.
  5. Acknowledge the reconstructed state, refresh stale elements, and preserve the incoming handoff as history when producing the next one.

Illustrative example

A maker stops after a replay regression fails. Its handoff includes the candidate hash, current contract revision, failing request, protected expectation, and remaining attempt budget. The next worker discovers that a policy delta arrived after the checkpoint. It preserves the old failure record but refreshes the affected assumptions before attempting a repair, instead of resuming from a vague “almost finished” summary.

What to check

  • The recipient can explain the current state and next permitted decision from the handoff.
  • Referenced evidence matches the relevant revisions and preserves open questions.
  • Budget and permission constraints survive the transfer without silent expansion or reset.

Expected outputs

  • A versioned handoff record with evidence locators.
  • A recipient freshness check and reconciled continuation state.

Risks and failure modes

  • Overcompressed summaries can erase the diagnosis that justified the next attempt.
  • Successor agents may treat historical state as current authorization merely because it persisted.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • System Understanding, Context and Persistent Memory — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:062 · Research Artifact Preservation
  • PAT:047 · Context Engineering
  • PAT:020 · File-System as State Machine

PAT:073PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Multi-Mode Agent

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Give one agent distinct functional modes such as inspection, planning, bounded implementation, and checking, with appropriate inputs and enforced permissions for each. Record mode transitions in the controller. Changing a role prompt can change the requested task, but the surrounding system must supply the actual access boundary and preserve accountability.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Avoid exposing every capability throughout a session when different stages need different actions and evidence.

When to use it

  • A workflow alternates between read-oriented investigation and a narrowly writable implementation stage.
  • One model can perform several functions while the controller retains explicit scope and transition rules.

When to avoid it

  • A prompt-only role change would be presented as real permission isolation or independent acceptance.

Before you start

  • A controller that can enforce actual tool and artifact permissions.
  • Defined mode inputs, outputs, transition conditions, and decision owners.

How to apply it

  1. Define modes by their engineering purpose and necessary operations rather than by impressive role names.
  2. Assign the least access needed for each mode and protect authoritative contracts and acceptance expectations from the maker.
  3. Require explicit current inputs and a recorded controller decision when entering a mode or expanding permitted action.
  4. Keep the task contract, remaining budget, and evidence history stable across mode transitions.
  5. Route the resulting candidate and findings to the responsible checker or owner without letting a mode label grant acceptance.

Illustrative example

An assistant inspects a repository with read access, then proposes a plan. After the controller admits the plan, implementation mode can write only candidate files. Checking reads protected expectations and writes a separate result. These transitions are recorded and enforced. Calling the final prompt “release manager” would add no ability or authority to publish the candidate.

What to check

  • Actual denied and allowed operations match the documented mode boundaries.
  • Each transition retains the applicable contract and resource history.
  • Mode outputs identify their evidence and do not claim a decision reserved for another role.

Expected outputs

  • A mode and permission specification with transition records.
  • Scoped candidate or finding artifacts from each admitted mode.

Risks and failure modes

  • A broad underlying credential can defeat apparently narrow prompt-level roles.
  • Reusing the maker’s interpretation in a checker mode can preserve circular verification.

PAT:074PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Anti-Sycophancy Enforcement

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Ask reviewers to challenge a candidate with evidence-backed objections rather than agree with its author or manufacture dissent. A useful finding identifies a defect, unsupported assumption, violated expectation, or concrete investigation. Requiring critical reasoning changes the review task; it does not by itself modify model training, incentives, or the independence of the evidence.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make review informative when agreement is socially easy or fluent candidate explanations are being accepted without challenge.

When to use it

  • Review comments mostly repeat the candidate’s rationale without examining consequential assumptions.
  • A proposed decision needs a reasoned challenge before an accountable owner evaluates the evidence.

When to avoid it

  • The process demands a quota of negative comments regardless of whether a concrete problem can be found.

Before you start

  • A known candidate and an authoritative behavior reference.
  • A finding format that distinguishes observed defects, hypotheses, and preferences.

How to apply it

  1. Ask the reviewer to identify the strongest consequential assumption in the candidate or its explanation.
  2. Require a source location, counterexample, violated requirement, or proposed diagnostic for each material objection.
  3. Classify the objection by evidence status rather than accepting confident criticism as a confirmed defect.
  4. Investigate actionable concerns and retain reasons when a finding is dismissed or remains unresolved.
  5. Allow a bounded no-additional-finding result and pass the full evidence record to the named acceptance owner.

Illustrative example

A reviewer first calls a storage refactor “too complex,” which supplies little actionable information. On closer examination, it identifies that replay calls the current policy evaluator instead of returning the stored response. The latter objection names a path and a protected expectation that can be tested. If no defect is established, the review should say so rather than inventing another objection to appear adversarial.

What to check

  • Material criticism contains a traceable claim and a useful way to examine it.
  • The record separates established failures from plausible but untested concerns.
  • Acceptance depends on evidence and authority, not on the number of objections or agreements.

Expected outputs

  • An evidence-linked challenge record.
  • Resolved findings, investigations, and bounded remaining uncertainty.

Risks and failure modes

  • Performative disagreement can produce expensive false positives and discourage useful collaboration.
  • A persuasive critic can be overtrusted for the same reasons as a persuasive maker.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:075PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Convergence Review

Family. Critique, Review and Trust

Compare a proposal, a reasoned challenge, and their supporting evidence to resolve a bounded review question. Preserve objections and the basis for any changed position instead of keeping only the final agreement. Convergence is useful when the reasons survive checking; agreement between models alone neither calibrates confidence nor proves that the candidate is correct.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make a disputed engineering decision inspectable without treating consensus as an independent acceptance oracle.

When to use it

  • Reviewers disagree about a specific tradeoff, defect hypothesis, or interpretation that available evidence could help resolve.
  • A second perspective may expose an assumption the initial reviewer did not examine.

When to avoid it

  • The missing ingredient is an authoritative requirement or an executable check, and discussion would merely defer obtaining it.

Before you start

  • A bounded question, shared candidate revision, and accessible evidence.
  • A stop condition and a named owner for unresolved decisions.

How to apply it

  1. Record the initial proposal and its evidence before exposing it to the challenger’s reasoning.
  2. Ask the challenger for a concrete counterargument and distinguish competing facts from differing preferences.
  3. Identify the observation, source, or owner decision that could discriminate between the positions.
  4. Perform or obtain that check, then record which claims changed and which objections remain.
  5. Stop when the bounded question is answered or no useful new evidence emerges; escalate unresolved consequential disagreement.

Illustrative example

One reviewer accepts a replay refactor because current tests pass. Another argues that the tests expect the wrong policy revision. They inspect the authorized historical-response contract and run an independently specified case. The first position changes because of that evidence. Had both reviewers initially agreed with the flawed tests, their consensus would not have made the replay behavior acceptable.

What to check

  • The final position is traceable to checked reasons rather than a vote count.
  • Dissenting claims and unresolved questions remain available to the decision owner.
  • The review stops according to the question and evidence, not a requirement that all models agree.

Expected outputs

  • A proposal, challenge, and evidence-resolution record.
  • A bounded conclusion or named escalation.

Risks and failure modes

  • Repeated discussion can amplify shared assumptions while appearing to increase confidence.
  • Removing dissent from the final summary can hide residual uncertainty from the reviewer.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Code Review and Trust Calibration — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:076PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Gate-Enforced Progression

Family. Intentions, Contracts and Specifications

Advance a candidate only when the relevant explicit predicates and decision rights are satisfied. Keep structural checks, behavioral verification, authorization, and acceptance distinct, and reopen affected gates when their inputs change. Use gates to support small iterative changes; a fixed sequence of documents or a green structural report is not a substitute for accountable judgment.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Make the reason for progression or hold specific enough to verify and act on without freezing the development lifecycle.

When to use it

  • Several stages depend on current contracts, protected checks, evidence, and named decisions.
  • Candidates arrive with stale results or pass through review because expected files merely exist.

When to avoid it

  • A gate imposes artifacts that do not answer a relevant obligation or duplicates an already adequate approval mechanism.

Before you start

  • Defined gate inputs, predicates, outcome states, and decision authorities.
  • Versioned canonical records with identifiable dependent evidence.

How to apply it

  1. Specify which observable conditions are machine-checkable and which decisions require an authenticated accountable owner.
  2. Bind each gate result to the actual contract, candidate, oracle, and environment revisions it examined.
  3. Return named failures or holds with a useful corrective action, preserving distinctions between missing evidence and missing authority.
  4. When an authorized delta changes a premise, invalidate affected results and reopen only the relevant work with required regressions.
  5. Generate compatibility views from the canonical record and route edits to those views back as proposed deltas.

Illustrative example

A candidate passes schema checks and its test suite, but the contract revision changed after the tests ran. The progression gate holds the stale evidence and identifies the affected expectations. The maker refreshes the candidate and checks; the authorized reviewer still decides acceptance. An old-format tracking sheet is regenerated from the contract rather than becoming a second path to approval.

What to check

  • Gate outcomes identify exact checked revisions and named predicates.
  • A missing authority decision cannot be satisfied by a populated text field alone.
  • Changed inputs reopen affected results while preserving the prior decision history.

Expected outputs

  • A predicate and authority specification.
  • Version-bound progression, hold, and reopening records.

Risks and failure modes

  • A structural pass can be mistaken for complete verification or release permission.
  • Rigid gate ceremonies can obstruct legitimate small increments and encourage workarounds.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Intentions, Contracts and Iterative Change — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:077PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Security Pipeline

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Compose security checks around named threats, protected assets, and decision owners across the application and its development tools. Keep scanning, dependency review, permission enforcement, negative testing, and release judgment distinct but connected. The pipeline records what each control actually examined and what remains unresolved; completing its stages is not a universal security guarantee.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Ensure that useful individual security signals contribute to an inspectable decision instead of becoming disconnected green status indicators.

When to use it

  • A change introduces untrusted input, new dependencies, external tools, or consequential data flows.
  • Current security checks run independently without a clear connection to threats and release decisions.

When to avoid it

  • A generic pipeline would be claimed to satisfy a specialized security obligation without examining the relevant environment.

Before you start

  • An explicit threat and asset inventory for both product and development chain.
  • Owners for controls, exceptions, findings, and the final operational decision.

How to apply it

  1. Map each consequential threat to the boundary it could cross and the evidence needed to examine it.
  2. Select complementary controls such as source review, dependency provenance, permissions, scanning, and targeted negative cases.
  3. Place permission enforcement before effects occur, independently of whether a content scanner raises a finding.
  4. Bind results to the candidate and control configuration, classify failures, and preserve denied actions without exposing sensitive contents.
  5. Assemble the findings and residual gaps for accountable review; reassess affected controls when tools or permissions change.

Illustrative example

An import feature receives malformed-input checks, dependency review, and a data-flow examination. The assistant’s runtime separately denies unapproved outbound calls and writes to protected expectations. A text scanner reports no suspicious instruction in the fixture, but that result cannot unlock the denied network operation. The reviewer sees the purpose and limit of each control rather than a single undifferentiated security badge.

What to check

  • Each selected control answers a named threat question and records its scope.
  • Permission denials remain effective when a scanner misses suspicious content.
  • The final decision retains unresolved findings, control versions, and accountable ownership.

Expected outputs

  • A threat-to-control map and candidate-bound results.
  • A security decision record with residual uncertainty.

Risks and failure modes

  • Correlated or overlapping scanners can leave the same important boundary unexamined.
  • Changes to execution configuration can invalidate earlier results without changing application code.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:051 · Security-First Development
  • PAT:078 · Prompt Injection Scanning
  • PAT:079 · Supply-Chain Risk Audit

PAT:078PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Prompt Injection Scanning

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Inspect repository text, retrieved material, and tool outputs for content that attempts to redirect an assistant beyond the task’s authority. Treat findings as signals for examination, preserving the source context and an appropriate response. Since scanning can miss or misclassify content, independently enforced tool permissions must still limit the effects of any resulting action.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Expose suspicious attempts to promote lower-trust task data into operational instructions without relying on detection as the sole defense.

When to use it

  • An assistant reads external pages, repository prose, issues, or tool outputs before deciding its next action.
  • A workflow needs triage and evidence for suspicious instruction-like content.

When to avoid it

  • Scanning would be used to justify otherwise unauthorized access or to certify arbitrary content as safe.

Before you start

  • Known data and instruction boundaries with a bounded response policy.
  • External enforcement of permitted tools, targets, and effects.

How to apply it

  1. Identify the lower-trust input surfaces the task actually consumes and retain their origin and version where possible.
  2. Inspect for attempts to claim higher authority, redirect the objective, or request out-of-scope operations.
  3. Record suspected passages with enough context to assess whether they are malicious instructions, quotations, or legitimate task data.
  4. Keep the content as data and route material findings for review without executing the suspicious request to investigate it.
  5. Exercise relevant permission denials independently of scanner results and record the limits of the detection coverage.

Illustrative example

A repository note tells an assistant to send local configuration to an external endpoint before continuing a build. Scanning flags the instruction and preserves its source locator. Even if a paraphrase evades that rule, the runtime still denies the unapproved outbound operation. The useful evidence consists of the suspicious-content finding and the enforced denial, which answer different questions.

What to check

  • Findings identify the input source and the proposed authority crossing.
  • False positives can be classified without silently promoting quoted content to instructions.
  • A missed finding cannot by itself enable an operation outside the permission envelope.

Expected outputs

  • A source-linked scan and triage record.
  • Independent boundary-check evidence and coverage limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • Overbroad rules may flag legitimate documentation and create expensive review noise.
  • Treating a scan as a permission check can leave uncontrolled effects when detection fails.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:079PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Supply-Chain Risk Audit

Family. Security of the Toolchain and Its Effects

Review the identity, provenance, necessity, permissions, and update path of executable dependencies, including packages, tool servers, hooks, and skills. Track the actual resolved artifacts and their transitive dependencies where relevant. A familiar name or a pinned version reduces some ambiguity, but neither supplies a permanent list of trustworthy tools or proves safe behavior.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Examine the transition from a suggested dependency to code allowed to install, execute, access data, or influence the agent.

When to use it

  • A generated change proposes a new package, tool integration, hook, or skill.
  • An existing dependency changes version, source, resolved artifact, or requested permissions.

When to avoid it

  • A successful name lookup or manifest check would be presented as sufficient evidence for unrestricted execution.

Before you start

  • An inventory of executable dependencies and their approved purpose.
  • A decision owner with access to artifact identity and permission information.

How to apply it

  1. Question whether the new dependency is needed or an already approved capability can meet the requirement.
  2. Verify the exact name, source, version, resolved artifact identity, and relevant transitive dependency record.
  3. Examine installation and execution behavior, requested access, and changes to automatic hooks or tool entry points.
  4. Approve only the necessary scope through the appropriate process and record the review basis and unresolved concerns.
  5. Reassess material updates or permission changes, preserving the previous manifest for rollback and investigation.

Illustrative example

An assistant proposes a similarly named package to simplify parsing. The reviewer checks the actual registry identity and artifact, then notices an installation step that executes additional code. The team may reject the dependency or admit a narrower reviewed alternative. Its existence in a registry and a passing application test would not have answered the installation or provenance questions.

What to check

  • The reviewed identity matches the artifact that will actually resolve or execute.
  • Requested permissions and automatic actions are understood within the intended task scope.
  • Material changes trigger renewed review rather than inheriting approval from a familiar name.

Expected outputs

  • A dependency and permission manifest with review provenance.
  • An update, rejection, or bounded admission decision.

Risks and failure modes

  • A floating or indirect dependency can change execution without a visible application diff.
  • A hash match can confirm bytes while leaving publisher identity or behavioral safety unestablished.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Securing Generated Code and Agent Runtimes — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:080PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Adversarial Agent Pattern

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Assign a checker the bounded task of finding violations of an authorized contract. Separate the critical stance, the origin of expected results, artifact permissions, and acceptance authority. Give findings their own output channel and protect the oracle from the maker as well as the checker. Another agent is a possible reviewer, not automatically independent evidence.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Create a focused search for counterexamples while preserving the boundary between producing, examining, and accepting a candidate.

When to use it

  • A plausible candidate could pass self-tests based on the maker’s own mistaken interpretation.
  • A consequential invariant benefits from a dedicated search for negative cases or unexpected changes.

When to avoid it

  • The checker lacks an independently grounded expectation or would be allowed to negotiate a weaker contract with the maker.

Before you start

  • A known candidate and authorized expected behavior with source provenance.
  • Protected contract and oracle artifacts, separate findings output, and a named acceptance owner.

How to apply it

  1. Define the invariant or risk the checker should challenge and the limits of its investigation.
  2. Provide independently grounded expectations and relevant context without using the maker’s conclusion as the oracle.
  3. Enforce read and write permissions so the maker cannot rewrite the expectation and the checker cannot silently alter the candidate.
  4. Require a concrete counterexample, violated obligation, or identifiable evidence gap for a material finding.
  5. Return diagnosed failures for bounded repair and policy ambiguities to the owner; retain the evidence for accountable acceptance.

Illustrative example

A maker’s self-test accepts a replay response recomputed under current policy. A checker reads the separately approved historical-response invariant and constructs the conflicting case. The maker may repair candidate code but cannot edit that protected expectation. The checker records a reproducible failure; it does not independently authorize a policy change or declare the repaired service ready for release.

What to check

  • Expected results have an origin independent of the candidate’s observed answer.
  • Permission checks protect the oracle against writes by both relevant roles.
  • Findings are traceable and the resulting state preserves separate acceptance authority.

Expected outputs

  • A scoped counterexample or evidence-gap report.
  • A candidate-bound check result and repair or escalation path.

Risks and failure modes

  • Two differently named agents may reproduce the same circular reasoning.
  • An unbounded critic can create indefinite repair cycles without new diagnostic evidence.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:027 · Maker–Checker: Separate Production from Acceptance
  • PAT:044 · Test-Driven AI Development
  • PAT:082 · Evidence-Pack Provenance

PAT:081PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

One-Item-Per-Cycle

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Organize each execution cycle around one semantic work item with a defined acceptance question. Load its current contract and budget, attempt bounded work, observe the result, and checkpoint a named next state before admitting another item. This is a temporal specialization of small verifiable increments, not a rule that one cycle must touch only one file or make one tool call.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Keep attempts, diagnoses, resource consumption, and stopping decisions attributable to one coherent outcome at a time.

When to use it

  • An autonomous loop drifts among unrelated tasks or loses track of which failure it is trying to repair.
  • A resumed worker needs a clear item and a reliable transition before starting further work.

When to avoid it

  • The proposed item is defined only by an arbitrary file boundary and cannot be checked as a coherent behavior.

Before you start

  • A small verifiable work item with current contract and checks.
  • Persistent state and externally maintained resource counters.

How to apply it

  1. Load one item, its applicable contract, candidate state, current diagnostic, and remaining budget.
  2. Admit only actions needed for that item, recording relevant observations and newly discovered dependencies.
  3. Run the focused check and required regressions; distinguish a diagnosed failure from an unrelated issue.
  4. Checkpoint the candidate, evidence, consumed resources, and a named result such as ready for review, stopped, or escalated.
  5. Begin another item only through an explicit allocation or resumption decision, keeping unresolved follow-ups separate.

Illustrative example

A cycle implements revised request routing while preserving replay behavior, touching several related files. A failing unrelated report test is recorded as a separate issue rather than becoming the cycle’s new objective. The checkpoint identifies the routing candidate, its own verification result, and remaining resources. The controller can then request review or assign another item without losing the first decision trail.

What to check

  • The cycle’s actions and evidence relate to one stated acceptance question.
  • Its checkpoint supports reconstruction after interruption without resetting consumed resources.
  • Unrelated findings become explicit follow-ups rather than unrecorded scope expansion.

Expected outputs

  • A cycle trace tied to one semantic item.
  • A durable checkpoint and named continuation or stop state.

Risks and failure modes

  • An overly broad item can hide many changes behind a nominally single task.
  • Treating every tool call as a separate cycle can fragment evidence and obscure the coherent outcome.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

PAT:082PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Evidence-Pack Provenance

Family. Tests, Oracles and Acceptance Evidence

Bind verification evidence to the exact candidate, authorized intention, oracle, policy, and environment it concerns. Preserve source artifacts, producing process, commands, outcomes, time, and unverified scope in a manifest. Integrity checks help detect mismatched or changed bytes, while separate execution and identity controls must establish who produced the evidence and whether its claims are trustworthy.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Let a reviewer determine whether an evidence pack actually applies to the candidate and decision currently under consideration.

When to use it

  • Checks are performed across sessions, services, or participants and their results must survive a handoff.
  • A candidate or requirement changes after a previously passing report was produced.

When to avoid it

  • A checksum-only manifest would be claimed to authenticate a producer or certify acceptance.

Before you start

  • Identifiable candidate, contract, oracle, policy, and environment revisions.
  • Permitted evidence storage and a trustworthy process for recording actual execution.

How to apply it

  1. Record the invocation, input revisions, environment, producing process, timestamp, and result for each material check.
  2. Retain the relevant raw artifacts and give each a stable locator and digest where appropriate.
  3. Assemble a manifest that maps the claims to those artifacts and states the checks and uncertainty outside its scope.
  4. Before use, compare the recorded revisions with the current decision inputs and separately verify any required producer or approval identity.
  5. Hold stale or incomplete evidence, retain it as history, and rerun the affected checks rather than renaming an old report as current.

Illustrative example

A report shows that replay checks passed for candidate A under contract revision one. The candidate changes to B before review. Even if the old report’s digest still matches its stored bytes, it does not establish B’s behavior. The reviewer holds the bundle until relevant checks are rerun and the new manifest identifies the actual inputs and producer.

What to check

  • Every material verification claim resolves to a recorded invocation and relevant artifacts.
  • The pack matches the candidate and authority revisions used for the present decision.
  • Integrity, producer identity, execution trust, and acceptance authority remain separate checks.

Expected outputs

  • A version-bound evidence manifest and retained artifacts.
  • A freshness and provenance result with explicit limitations.

Risks and failure modes

  • A file named as a passing result can conceal that no trustworthy execution produced it.
  • Reusing current-looking metadata around old artifacts can launder stale evidence into a new review.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Independent Verification and the Oracle Problem — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

PAT:083PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Budget-Gated Autonomy

Family. Delegation, Execution and Stopping

Check resource limits before admitting the next autonomous action, using conservative allowances for attempts, calls, elapsed time, and cost. Persist consumed resources across interruptions, retries, model switches, and scheduler restarts. Budget bounds the permitted execution opportunity; unused resources cannot authorize a forbidden action, resolve missing intention, or convert a candidate into an accepted outcome.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Prevent an apparently cheap repeated step from accumulating into unbounded work or resetting its resource history whenever execution resumes.

When to use it

  • An agent can repeatedly invoke tools, regenerate candidates, or continue across sessions.
  • The next step has uncertain cost or a loop lacks an explicit stop decision.

When to avoid it

  • A numerical allowance would be used to permit actions outside the task’s authority or protected boundaries.

Before you start

  • A controller-owned resource ledger and clock.
  • Defined resource limits, a reservation policy, and an owner for escalation.

How to apply it

  1. Choose the relevant resource dimensions and limits for the task, including mandatory checking and shutdown obligations.
  2. Before each action, estimate or enforce a conservative maximum allowance and deny admission when it cannot fit.
  3. Reserve the allowance in shared persistent state so concurrent or restarted attempts cannot each spend the same remainder.
  4. Reconcile actual consumption after execution, preserving attempt identity and unresolved reservations when completion is uncertain.
  5. Stop or escalate when limits are reached or unbounded actions are proposed; renew a budget only through the authorized decision path.

Illustrative example

A worker has enough remaining time for one bounded repair and its checks, but not for an open-ended dependency installation. The controller admits the repair and records the reservation before execution. If the worker restarts, the reservation and earlier attempts remain visible. A successful result still goes to review; remaining budget does not let the worker publish it.

What to check

  • Admission checks all relevant resource dimensions before execution.
  • Restart and concurrent-attempt checks cannot silently reset or duplicate the available allowance.
  • Stops distinguish exhausted budget from missing authority or verification failure.

Expected outputs

  • A persistent budget and reservation ledger.
  • Admission, reconciliation, and stop decisions tied to attempts.

Risks and failure modes

  • Tracking expenditure only afterwards can reveal overspend without having prevented it.
  • A non-atomic ledger or ambiguous completion can admit duplicate work against the same remaining budget.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Limits and Capability of Coding Agents — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

Related practices

  • PAT:021 · Tool Call Budget
  • PAT:033 · Budget and Observability: Price the Next Attempt
  • PAT:084 · Escalation Protocol

PAT:084PAT · PracticesEnglish guidance

Escalation Protocol

Family. Coordination, Governance and Adoption

Return work through an explicit escalation when a required decision, permission, diagnostic, or resource is unavailable. Preserve the candidate and evidence, name the blocked outcome and responsible authority, and ask for the smallest decision that can resolve the block. Escalation is a recorded workflow result; it does not authorize acceptance simply because the execution budget has ended.

Apply this practice: steps, example and verification

Purpose

Turn a stopped or disputed task into an actionable decision without losing evidence or encouraging unbounded retries.

When to use it

  • A consequential requirement is unresolved, a permitted route is unavailable, or repeated failures lack a useful new diagnosis.
  • The task reaches a resource limit, permission boundary, ownership conflict, or required review that the worker cannot resolve.

When to avoid it

  • The worker can resolve a routine implementation issue safely within existing authority and available evidence.

Before you start

  • Named responsibilities for intention, permissions, verification, coordination, and acceptance.
  • A preserved task state and a way to deliver the decision request through the permitted workflow.

How to apply it

  1. Classify the blocking condition and record a named state rather than treating every stop as failure or completion.
  2. Preserve the current candidate, applicable revisions, attempts, diagnostic evidence, remaining resources, and affected scope.
  3. Identify the authority able to decide the issue and state the smallest concrete question or action needed.
  4. Describe eligible options and their consequences without recommending an unsupported waiver of mandatory controls.
  5. Resume only after the relevant decision is recorded and stale assumptions are reconciled, or close the task with its explicit disposition.

Illustrative example

A maker receives a second rejection saying the patch is wrong but no failing case or violated rule. It preserves both candidates and review messages, stops further regeneration under the agreed retry policy, and asks the verification owner for a traceable diagnostic. The owner may supply a counterexample or route an unresolved policy question onward. The stop never turns the latest green self-test into acceptance.

What to check

  • The escalation identifies an actionable question and the appropriate decision authority.
  • A successor can reconstruct the block and relevant evidence without repeating the whole investigation.
  • Resumption records the decision and preserves resource, permission, and contract constraints.

Expected outputs

  • A named escalation or stop record with evidence.
  • A decision-linked resumption, reassignment, or closure outcome.

Risks and failure modes

  • Vague requests for approval can burden the wrong person while leaving the real decision unresolved.
  • Repeated retries or implicit waivers can conceal a missing authority boundary.

Read with the published NDSE2 chapters

  • Teams, Governance and the Engineering Organization — Thematic chapter guidance
  • Choosing Practices and Recognizing Their Limits — Practice selection and proportionality

These are editorial reading guides. A practice descriptor does not represent a literal source citation or an independent study.

  • PAT:026 · Run Until Done: Retry Against Reality
  • PAT:032 · Multi-Loop Coordination: One Owner per Target
